ideas.statement: For 1406 test queries on ArguAna, Table 4 gives NDCG@10 GPT-AC 0.327, BM25 0.315, GZIP 0.073, DPR 0.175. GPT-AC is highest among the listed systems.
ideas.conditions: BM25 top-100 candidate reranking; best GPT-AC metric combination reported.
validity_flags: Table 4 GPT-AC result differs from the maximum shown in Table 5 (0.186 for TREC-NEWS; 0.307 for ArguAna). No reconciliation supplied.

ideas.title: BioASQ reranking effectiveness
ideas.statement: For 500 test queries on BioASQ, Table 4 gives NDCG@10 GPT-AC 0.517, BM25 0.465, GZIP 0.157, DPR 0.127. GPT-AC is highest among the listed systems.
ideas.conditions: BM25 top-100 candidate reranking; best GPT-AC metric combination reported.

ideas.title: FiQA-2018 reranking effectiveness
ideas.statement: For 648 test queries on FiQA-2018, Table 4 gives NDCG@10 GPT-AC 0.239, BM25 0.236, GZIP 0.032, DPR 0.112. GPT-AC is highest among the listed systems.
ideas.conditions: BM25 top-100 candidate reranking; best GPT-AC metric combination reported.

ideas.title: Zero-shot reranking of BM25 candidates
ideas.statement: Retrieve the top 100 passages using BM25 with Elasticsearch, then rerank with GPT-AC on TREC-COVID, TREC-NEWS, SciFact, BioASQ, FiQA-2018 and ArguAna. Compare NDCG@10 to the original BM25 ordering, GZIP and a BERT-based DPR model fine-tuned on MS MARCO. Table 4 selects the best GPT-AC result among metric combinations.
ideas.conditions: Reranking the BM25 candidate set; DPR has supervised prior training. Selection protocol for the best metric combination is not detailed.
validity_flags: Best-of-metric reporting lacks a stated held-out metric-selection procedure.

ideas.title: SciFact reranking effectiveness
ideas.statement: For 300 test queries on SciFact, Table 4 gives NDCG@10 GPT-AC 0.648, BM25 0.665, GZIP 0.053, DPR 0.318. BM25 is higher than GPT-AC.
ideas.conditions: BM25 top-100 candidate reranking; best GPT-AC metric combination reported.

ideas.title: TREC-COVID reranking effectiveness
ideas.statement: For 50 test queries on TREC-COVID, Table 4 gives NDCG@10 GPT-AC 0.694, BM25 0.656, GZIP 0.447, DPR 0.332. GPT-AC is highest among the listed systems.
ideas.conditions: BM25 top-100 candidate reranking; best GPT-AC metric combination reported.

ideas.title: TREC-NEWS reranking effectiveness
ideas.statement: For 57 test queries on TREC-NEWS, Table 4 gives NDCG@10 GPT-AC 0.225, BM25 0.398, GZIP 0.142, DPR 0.161. BM25 is higher than GPT-AC.
ideas.conditions: BM25 top-100 candidate reranking; best GPT-AC metric combination reported.
validity_flags: Table 4 GPT-AC result differs from the maximum shown in Table 5 (0.186 for TREC-NEWS; 0.307 for ArguAna). No reconciliation supplied.

ideas.title: Reversible conversion length and claimed optimal learning metric
ideas.statement: Equation (11) defines E_U(x,y)=min{|p|:U(x,p)=y,U(y,p)=x}; erasing this program is said to cost |p|kT. Equation (12), attributed to Bennett et al. [3], states E_U(x,y)=E(x,y)+O(1), and the authors use ideal E minimality to motivate M_max for few-shot learning.
validity_flags: E_U is defined in program bits although the preceding text calls it minimum energy. The cited conversion equivalence has precision/constant subtleties; the original Information Distance abstract describes logarithmic additive terms. This does not establish task accuracy optimality for normalized finite-model C distances.

ideas.title: SBERT is a supervised reference baseline
ideas.statement: The authors include SBERT as a reference while excluding it from their human-like few-shot model category, because it was fine-tuned on one billion high-quality labeled sentence pairs. It exceeds GPT-AC on the Medical and Banking77 one-shot results, despite GPT-AC beating the listed fine-tuned GPT/BERT baselines.
ideas.conditions: Comparison involves differing prior supervised training; do not interpret all-baseline superiority from the paper’s abstract.

ideas.title: Qwen2.5-VL hierarchical annotation at two timescales
ideas.statement: Yan uses Qwen2.5-VL for hierarchical captions, with typical one-minute world traversals and three-second local clips, labeling 98 million training frames.
ideas.conditions: This is a selected annotated subset of the larger 400M-frame collection.

ideas.title: Parallel code-length evaluation with causal attention
ideas.statement: A full tokenized sequence can be passed through a causally masked GPT once to obtain all next-token distributions for code-length computation; a sliding-window technique is proposed for other generative language models including encoder-decoder architectures.
ideas.conditions: Single-pass claim is for forward-only attention and sequences within the usable context window; broader architecture applicability is proposed, not experimentally demonstrated here.

ideas.title: Unverified pretraining-leakage explanation for SST5
ideas.statement: The authors hypothesize that GPT-prompt’s better SST5 result may reflect data leakage during GPT pretraining because SST5 is a common benchmark.
validity_flags: Explicit author hypothesis; no leakage audit or evidence demonstrating contamination is presented.

ideas.title: STS-12 semantic-similarity result
ideas.statement: On STS-12 (3,108 test pairs), GPT-AC reports Spearman rho×100 40.2, compared with GZIP 50.4, GPT embeddings 5.4, and BERT embeddings 30.9. GZIP outperforms GPT-AC on this dataset.
ideas.conditions: Reported correlations for the specified test subset; method does not supply significance tests.

ideas.title: STS-13 semantic-similarity result
ideas.statement: On STS-13 (1,500 test pairs), GPT-AC reports Spearman rho×100 66.0, compared with GZIP 48.4, GPT embeddings 14.6, and BERT embeddings 59.9. GPT-AC is highest among these four baselines.
ideas.conditions: Reported correlations for the specified test subset; method does not supply significance tests.

ideas.title: STS-14 semantic-similarity result
ideas.statement: On STS-14 (3,750 test pairs), GPT-AC reports Spearman rho×100 55.3, compared with GZIP 43.3, GPT embeddings 10.9, and BERT embeddings 47.7. GPT-AC is highest among these four baselines.
ideas.conditions: Reported correlations for the specified test subset; method does not supply significance tests.

ideas.title: STS-15 semantic-similarity result
ideas.statement: On STS-15 (3,000 test pairs), GPT-AC reports Spearman rho×100 70.3, compared with GZIP 59.1, GPT embeddings 9.6, and BERT embeddings 60.3. GPT-AC is highest among these four baselines.
ideas.conditions: Reported correlations for the specified test subset; method does not supply significance tests.

ideas.title: STS-16 semantic-similarity result
ideas.statement: On STS-16 (1,186 test pairs), GPT-AC reports Spearman rho×100 69.5, compared with GZIP 59.4, GPT embeddings 26.8, and BERT embeddings 60.3. GPT-AC is highest among these four baselines.
ideas.conditions: Reported correlations for the specified test subset; method does not supply significance tests.

ideas.title: Semantic textual similarity evaluation and baselines
ideas.statement: Evaluate STS-12 through STS-16 and STS-b with Spearman rank correlation times 100 against human relatedness labels. GPT-2 uses last-token embeddings, BERT uses average token embeddings, both with cosine similarity; GZIP uses normalized compression distance following prior compression-learning work.
ideas.conditions: STS-b labels range 0–5; no task fine-tuning for these embedding baselines.

ideas.title: STS-b semantic-similarity result
ideas.statement: On STS-b (1,379 test pairs), GPT-AC reports Spearman rho×100 55.0, compared with GZIP 50.7, GPT embeddings 12.4, and BERT embeddings 47.3. GPT-AC is highest among these four baselines.
ideas.conditions: Reported correlations for the specified test subset; method does not supply significance tests.

ideas.title: Universal information distance
ideas.statement: The paper defines M_UID(x,y)=max{K(x|y),K(y|x)} and attributes its optimality for the human-like setting to information-distance theory grounded in the von-Neumann–Landauer principle.
ideas.conditions: Ideal uncomputable Kolmogorov complexities; optimality does not automatically transfer to finite pretrained-model approximations.

ideas.title: Claimed minimality of universal information distance
ideas.statement: Theorem 1 states E(x,y)=max{K(x|y),K(y|x)} is an admissible metric and satisfies E(x,y)≤D(x,y)+c for every admissible D, with a constant c. The paper cites Bennett et al. as the source and reproduces a proof.
ideas.conditions: Ideal algorithmic information theory statement, not a guarantee for GPT-AC distances.
validity_flags: Printed exact metric and computability wording is stronger than justified; Kolmogorov metrics require additive-constant and diagonal conventions.

ideas.title: Triangle and density arguments in the appendix
ideas.statement: The proof derives triangle behavior through K(z|x)<K(y,z|x)<K(y|x)+K(z|x,y)<K(y|x)+K(z|y)≤E(x,y)+E(y,z), and density through sum_(y≠x)2^(-E(x,y))≤sum_(y≠x)2^(-K(y|x))≤1 using Kraft’s inequality.
validity_flags: Conditional-complexity inequalities omit additive constants and are not generally exact strict inequalities. Identity is not established by the displayed proof. The following minimality paragraph prints sum 2^(D(x,y))≤1, a missing-minus-sign error inconsistent with the density definition.

ideas.title: Coding lemma invoked to show universality
ideas.statement: Lemma 1 asserts that for every upper-semicomputable f(x,y) obeying sum_y 2^(-f(x,y))≤1, K(y|x)<f(x,y). It is used to bound both conditional complexities by a competing admissible distance.
ideas.conditions: Quoted as the source’s formal claim.
validity_flags: The lemma’s printed strict inequality omits a machine/function-dependent additive coding constant; do not treat it as a constant-free result.

ideas.title: Zero-shot GPT prompt templates
ideas.statement: Table 6 supplies a CaseHOLD prompt containing the citing text and holdings 0–4, asking which holding is correct and ending with Answer; PIQA similarly supplies a goal and options 0–1, asks which is correct, and ends with Answer.
ideas.conditions: These are source evidence templates, not instructions to this research worker. Answer scoring and decoding details are not specified here.

ideas.title: Story generation through architectural design
ideas.statement: The paper asserts that no story-based dataset is available to learn the desired story-to-video mapping directly, motivating an architecture designed for changing prompt conditioning.
ideas.conditions: Source claim as of publication; no dataset-availability survey or impossibility proof is provided.

ideas.title: Unconditional MaskGIT for video prediction
ideas.statement: The BAIR/Kinetics latent prediction transformer uses 24 layers, 768 hidden units, 16 attention heads, 3072 MLP units, and .1 dropout and attention dropout.
ideas.conditions: Unconditional here describes training without assuming given frames or text; inference supplies initial-frame tokens.

ideas.title: Video duration extrapolation from short clips
ideas.statement: Phenaki is reported to generate videos lasting minutes although trained on clips lasting 1.4 seconds at 8 fps, and to compose concepts into open-domain outputs.
ideas.conditions: Qualitative capability claim; arbitrary duration is architectural extensibility, not a guarantee of sustained fidelity at every length.

ideas.title: Qualitative story transitions across changing prompts
ideas.statement: Figure 1 presents selected frames from one autoregressively generated video whose prompts change from a teddy bear swimming near San Francisco to underwater swimming with fish and then a panda; the source reports temporal coherence and short-path adaptation, visibly including teddy-to-panda morphing. Figure 5 additionally shows an astronaut walking through a puddle on Mars, dancing, walking a newly appearing dog, and watching fireworks with the dog.
ideas.conditions: Selected still frames are qualitative evidence. They show the intended sequence and changes, but cannot establish motion quality over the full video or population-level reliability.

ideas.title: Per-frame and fixed-length video encoder tradeoff
ideas.statement: Per-frame image encoders such as VQ-GAN support arbitrary lengths but leave temporally redundant tokens and practical compute limits; fixed-length video encoders such as VideoVQVAE reduce tokens but constrain video length.
ideas.conditions: Characterization of prior architectures cited as [12], [18], [54], [57], [52] and [49]; not a universal claim about every conceivable encoder.

ideas.title: C-ViViT patch and token geometry
ideas.statement: For x in R^((t_x+1)×h_x×w_x×c_x), the first frame uses w_p×h_p×c_p patches and remaining frames use t_p×w_p×h_p×c_p patches. With all channels together, t_z=t_x/t_p, w_z=w_x/w_p, h_z=h_x/h_p, giving (t_z+1)w_z h_z tokens. Flattened patches are projected to dimension d_z and arranged as (t_z+1)×(w_z h_z)×d_z.
ideas.conditions: Non-overlapping patches and divisible dimensions are implicit in the stated ratios. The final embedding-shape sentence drops +1 and says t_z×w_z×h_z×d_z; retain this source notation discrepancy rather than silently treating both as identical.

ideas.title: Spatial attention followed by causal temporal attention
ideas.statement: C-ViViT first applies all-to-all spatial transformer layers, then causal temporal transformer layers so spatial tokens observe previous-frame spatial tokens. The first frame is independently encoded, supporting image training and conditioning on initial frames.
ideas.conditions: The first image is patchified separately; causal temporal processing preserves prefix independence.

ideas.title: Reverse encoder decoding into pixels
ideas.statement: C-ViViT converts tokens into embeddings, applies the temporal transformer and then the spatial transformer, and uses one linear projection without activation to recover pixels.
ideas.conditions: Decoder is described as an upside-down version of the encoder.

ideas.title: Vector quantization and commitment loss
ideas.statement: The adopted VQ-VAE objective is L_VQ=||sg(z)-e||_2^2 + beta||z-sg(e)||_2^2. sg(x)=x with derivative zero, beta weights commitment, and the nearest codebook index is i=argmin_j ||z-E_j||_2^2.
ideas.conditions: Background objective from VQVAEs [45], used to learn discrete codes; equation applies to encoder output z and codebook E. Appendix B.1.1 sets beta=.25 and codebook size 8192.

ideas.title: Factorized and normalized codebook representations
ideas.statement: Phenaki adopts factorized and L2-normalized codes from ViT-VQGAN [58] to improve codebook usage and reconstruction quality.
ideas.conditions: An adopted component, not a new normalization method introduced in this source.

ideas.title: Weighted C-ViViT reconstruction objective
ideas.statement: C-ViViT minimizes L=L_VQ+0.1 L_Adv+0.1 L_IP+1.0 L_VP+1.0 L_2, combining quantization, StyleGAN adversarial loss, image perceptual loss, I3D-feature video perceptual loss, and pixel L2 reconstruction.
ideas.conditions: Image perceptual references [20,61], I3D [6], and StyleGAN [21] identify adopted feature/discriminator components. Appendix B.1.1 specifies a StyleGAN discriminator with blur resample and channel multiplier 1.

ideas.title: C-ViViT changes to factorized ViViT
ideas.statement: Relative to ViViT [1], C-ViViT removes spatial and temporal CLS tokens, runs the temporal transformer for every spatial token rather than only CLS outputs, and replaces all-to-all temporal attention with causal attention to support unlabeled reconstruction, images, variable frame counts and future extrapolation. The resulting C-ViViT compresses video spatially and temporally while remaining autoregressive in time, so one encoder-decoder supports variable video lengths within transformer token budgets.
ideas.conditions: Source attribution distinguishes the inherited factorized encoder from these adaptations.

ideas.title: Autoregressive token decoding cost motivates masked generation
ideas.statement: Prior text-to-image/video transformers predict tokens sequentially from encoded text, requiring a number of sampling steps linear in sequence length even with caching; the paper regards this as impractical for long video sequences.
ideas.conditions: Background motivation about sequential sampling steps; it does not establish total wall-clock complexity independent of model or attention costs.

ideas.title: Parallel token prediction with iterative remasking
ideas.statement: Inspired by MaskGIT [8], training samples gamma_i in [0,1], replaces ceil(gamma_i N) tokens with MASK, and predicts masked tokens conditioned on text and unmasked tokens. Inference begins fully masked, predicts unknown tokens in parallel, retains a beta_i proportion of predictions, and remasks the remainder.
ideas.conditions: Masking and sampling schedules follow MaskGIT. The paper gives typical 12–48 sampling steps, says more steps generally improve quality, and claims an order-of-magnitude reduction in steps over autoregressive sampling; this is not constant total compute for arbitrary video length.

ideas.title: Masked Visual Token Modeling objective
ideas.statement: Pretrained C-ViViT codebook IDs of shape (t_z+1)×w_z×h_z are flattened in raster order [58]. Adopted MVTM [8] minimizes L_mask=-sum_{i in [1,N],m_i=1} log p(a_i | a_barM,p), where m_i marks masked positions, a_barM is the masked sequence, and p is the text embedding.
ideas.conditions: Only masked tokens contribute to cross entropy; the source defines a_barM as the masked version, not a separate full unmasked target.

ideas.title: Classifier-free guidance through text dropout
ideas.statement: Phenaki drops the text condition 10% of the time during training and uses guidance scale lambda at inference to control text-generation alignment.
ideas.conditions: Adopted classifier-free guidance attributed to [16,59]; the source does not provide a guidance-combination formula.

ideas.title: One masked objective for image and video examples
ideas.statement: To combine image and video datasets, the model applies masking and MVTM only to the first w_z h_z tokens for a single image and to all video tokens for a full video. This implements the joint large-image/smaller-video corpus training proposed to transfer concept coverage into video generation.
ideas.conditions: Requires the independently encoded first frame; intended to transfer image-only concepts such as pencil-drawing style into video generation.

ideas.title: Extrapolating a video by re-encoding its final frames
ideas.statement: After generating a clip, Phenaki encodes its last K frames with C-ViViT, initializes MaskGIT with those tokens, and predicts remaining future tokens under either the same or a changed text input to create visual transitions. Figure 2 depicts shifting the time window while freezing the past prefix and predicting empty future tokens under the next text prompt.
ideas.conditions: §3.3 specifies N, typically 5 previously generated frames, for story continuation (the earlier passage calls the count K). Changing text is done at continuation steps, without story-supervision data.

ideas.title: Five-task evaluation and implementation
ideas.statement: The source evaluates text-to-video, text-plus-image-to-video, changing-text story generation, video quantization, and image-conditional video prediction; implementation uses JAX and FLAX.
ideas.conditions: Some evaluations are qualitative. JAX and FLAX references appear as unresolved [?] markers in the paper; no identifiers are inferred.

ideas.title: Main text-conditioned training configuration
ideas.statement: The default Phenaki has 1.8B parameters and trains on about 15M text-video pairs at 8 fps, about 50M text-image pairs, and about 400M LAION-400M pairs. The visualization model ran 1M steps at batch size 512 in less than five days, sampling 80% video and 10% from each image dataset.
ideas.conditions: Source-reported training cost; hardware is not specified in this passage, and unnamed 15M/50M corpora are not independently identified.

ideas.title: Game capture at 1920 by 1080
ideas.statement: The data collection engine renders 1920×1080 images using an NVIDIA RTX 4060 per engine.
ideas.conditions: Capture hardware; distinct from model-inference GPU.

ideas.title: No established text-to-video benchmark and unequal comparisons
ideas.statement: The source says text-to-video lacks an established benchmark and that comparisons to CogVideo demos are limited by scale (9B versus Phenaki 1.8B), different training data and unknown prompt representativeness.
ideas.conditions: As-of-publication assessment. The linked demo comparison is external evidence not reproduced or quantitatively validated in this extraction.

ideas.title: Zero-shot Kinetics-400 comparison
ideas.statement: At matched 0.9B scale, Phenaki trained with a 50% video/50% image mixture is evaluated zero-shot on Kinetics-400 while NUWA is fine-tuned there. Table 1 reports image/video FID respectively: T2V 82.13/14.65; SC 33.51/7.34; TFGAN 31.76/7.19; NUWA 28.46/7.05; Phenaki 37.74/3.84. Phenaki has the lowest video FID but a worse image FID than NUWA, SC and TFGAN.
ideas.conditions: Lower is better for both metrics. Table 1 labels its second metric FID Video, not FVD; do not conflate it with Table 2 FVD. Dataset training exposure differs; no uncertainty is supplied.

ideas.title: Image mixture trades dynamics for concept alignment
ideas.statement: Table 2 gives video CLIP/FID/FVD and image CLIP/FID for video/image mixtures: 100/0 yields .298/19.2/168.9 and .240/53.9; 80/20 yields .303/21.4/198.4 and .289/29.4; 50/50 yields .302/21.4/239.7 and .287/30.5. Adding images improves alignment and image FID but degrades video FVD versus video-only training.
ideas.conditions: Image evaluation uses about 40K LAION-400M images. CLIP is higher-better; FID and FVD lower-better. Source calls differences significant without reporting inferential tests or uncertainty. More image data is not monotonically better on alignment.

ideas.title: Can improved video data reduce the concept-dynamics tradeoff?
ideas.statement: The authors expect larger and higher-quality text-video datasets to improve the tradeoff between concept coverage obtained from images and motion quality learned from videos.
ideas.conditions: Prospective hypothesis, not a tested result in this paper.

ideas.title: Animating unseen photographs with a text prompt
ideas.statement: Using the same main model as §3.1, Phenaki conditions on unseen local photographs captured by the authors’ phones and related text prompts to generate a continuation. The source reports coherent motion following the prompts.
ideas.conditions: Qualitative experiment; unseen status is author-reported, and Figure 4 contains selected frames rather than a statistical evaluation.

ideas.title: Kinetics-600 prediction comparison
ideas.statement: Table 4 FVD values are Video Transformer 170.0±5.00; CogVideo 109.2; DVD-GAN-FP 69.1±0.78; Video VQ-VAE 64.3±2.04; CCVS 55.0±1.00; TrIVD-GAN-FP 25.7±0.66; Transframer 25.4; RaMViD 16.5; Video Diffusion 16.2±0.34; Phenaki 36.4±0.19. Phenaki improves over several older entries but trails four listed methods.
ideas.conditions: Kinetics-600: predict 11 frames from 5; FVD lower-better. The source does not define these ± quantities or number of repeats in this table.

ideas.title: Qualitative image-to-video style and concept transfer
ideas.statement: Figure 3 shows six text-conditioned examples: panda washing dishes with yellow gloves, panda in boxing gloves by Brandenburg Gate with fireworks, pencil-drawn headphone-wearing panda knitting, astronaut riding a horse on Mars at sunset, astronaut at a coral reef with fish, and cartoon astronaut high-fiving a bear. The paper reports that stylized video concepts transfer from image training because its video corpus lacks such stylized videos.
ideas.conditions: Six selected three-frame examples support qualitative composition and style claims. They do not establish exact prompt fidelity or verify that every composition was absent from training.

ideas.title: MiT reconstruction benchmark and per-frame baselines
ideas.statement: C-ViViT encoding/reconstruction is evaluated on Moments-in-Time (MiT) [29], described as approximately 802K training, 33K validation and 67K test videos at 25 fps, against per-frame ViT [58] and convolutional VQ-GAN [12] encoder-decoders.
ideas.conditions: These are source-reported native dataset sizes/rate; actual experiment downsampling and model matching appear in Appendix B.1.

ideas.title: Spatial versus spatiotemporal distribution metrics
ideas.statement: The paper uses FID [15] and FVD [44] to compare generated/reconstructed outputs with ground-truth distributions; FID ignores temporal coherence while FVD assesses video spatiotemporal dynamics.
ideas.conditions: These are distributional metrics, not per-example exact reconstruction or human semantic-alignment measures.

ideas.title: MiT reconstruction quality with fewer video tokens
ideas.statement: Table 3 reports FID/FVD/token count: Conv VQ-GAN 7.5/306.1/2560; Conv plus video loss 13.7/346.5/2560; ViT VQ-GAN 3.4/166.6/2560; ViT plus video loss 3.8/173.1/2560; C-ViViT 4.5/65.78/1536. C-ViViT has substantially lower FVD and 40% fewer tokens, with worse FID than the ViT baselines but better FID than the convolutional baselines. The introduction summarizes this as a reduction of 40% or more through temporal redundancy compression.
ideas.conditions: Baseline counts represent 10 frames while C-ViViT represents 11 because of its isolated initial frame. Lower is better. The paper’s blanket prose about per-frame models having better FID only fits ViT, not the convolutional rows. No uncertainty or significance test is reported.

ideas.title: Adding video perceptual loss does not fix per-frame encoders
ideas.statement: In Table 3, adding video loss worsens Conv VQ-GAN from FID/FVD 7.5/306.1 to 13.7/346.5 and ViT VQ-GAN from 3.4/166.6 to 3.8/173.1 while keeping 2560 tokens.
ideas.conditions: Observed MiT reconstruction ablation for these architectures and settings; not a general proof that video perceptual losses are harmful.

ideas.title: BAIR and Kinetics frame prediction tasks
ideas.statement: To evaluate learned representations beyond reconstruction, Phenaki predicts 15 frames from one given BAIR Robot Pushing frame and 11 frames from five given Kinetics-600 frames.
ideas.conditions: Image-conditioned tasks; details and baseline conditioning differences are in Tables 4–5 and Appendix B.2.

ideas.title: BAIR prediction comparison
ideas.statement: Table 5 FVD values are DVD-GAN 109.8; VideoGPT 103.3; TrIVD-GAN 103.3; Transframer 100.0; HARP 99.3; CCVS 99.0; Video Transformer 94.0; FitVid 93.6; MCVD 89.5; NUWA 86.9; RaMViD 84.2; Phenaki 97.0. Phenaki lies between CCVS and Video Transformer and trails five listed methods.
ideas.conditions: BAIR: predict 15 frames from 1; FVD lower-better. No error bars supplied.

ideas.title: Missing specialized prediction components
ideas.statement: Phenaki is not specifically designed for video prediction and lacks components such as U-Net skip connections that the source cites as helpful to prediction methods.
ideas.conditions: Authors offer this as context for benchmark performance; no skip-connection ablation on Phenaki is reported.

ideas.title: DALL-E and Parti discrete image token generation
ideas.statement: As described in related work, DALL-E [34] maps text tokens to VQ-VAE [45] image embeddings, while Parti [59] predicts ViT-VQGAN [58] tokens with a 21B-parameter transformer.
ideas.conditions: Background descriptions by this paper, not independent re-evaluation of those methods.

ideas.title: GODIVA local attention for long video-token sequences
ideas.statement: Related work describes GODIVA [52] as mapping text to image-VQVAE video tokens and using local attention to cope with the large number of multi-frame tokens.
ideas.conditions: Source inconsistency: §2.1 places [52] among fixed-length video-encoder methods, while §4 describes an image-based VQVAE. Both descriptions are preserved without resolving from memory.

ideas.title: NUWA versus NUWA-Infinity length handling
ideas.statement: The source describes NUWA [54] as generating fixed-size outputs and NUWA-Infinity [53] as adding a second autoregressive layer for variable-size images/videos; NUWA-Infinity also uses the previous frame during decoding.
ideas.conditions: Related-work characterization; Phenaki’s claimed distinction is explicit temporal redundancy compression rather than treating frames independently.

ideas.title: CogVideo uses image-model transfer to address video data scarcity
ideas.statement: The source describes CogVideo [18] as addressing scarce high-quality text-video data through pretrained text-to-image models.
ideas.conditions: Background method rationale; Phenaki’s joint training is a distinct implementation of sharing image information.

ideas.title: Video diffusion uses a 3D space-time pixel model
ideas.statement: VDM [17] replaces 2D image U-Nets with a 3D space-time model for pixel-space video diffusion. The source describes fixed-size videos and an autoregressive extension for longer output, but argues high sampling time makes that extension impractical.
ideas.conditions: Authors’ comparison; no matched wall-clock benchmark is presented here.

ideas.title: Families of prior video generation models
ideas.statement: The source surveys deterministic recurrent/convolutional [36,42,13,50], variational stochastic [2,10,46,3], discrete-representation [49,33,31], autoregressive [51,55,28,57], diffusion [47,14,56,19], flow [24] and adversarial [48,39,43,9,40,27] video methods.
ideas.conditions: A background taxonomy rather than separate experimental validation of each method; continuation qualifies their predominantly limited-domain scope.

ideas.title: Generated videos often do not fully match user intent
ideas.statement: The authors acknowledge that many generated samples will not perfectly correspond to the input caption or user intent.
ideas.conditions: Qualitative limitation with no mismatch rate quantified.

ideas.title: Potential creative time savings remain untested
ideas.statement: The authors suggest that users may save time even if only one generated sample matches their intent and foresee artistic and storytelling applications.
ideas.conditions: They explicitly state downstream applications were not explored; productivity benefits are hypotheses rather than user-study findings.

ideas.title: Synthetic video misuse and nonconsensual depictions
ideas.statement: The ethics statement identifies potential misuse for malicious fake content and videos of people without consent, even while noting that generated videos are not generally indistinguishable from real video.
ideas.conditions: Potential downstream risk analysis, not a reported misuse experiment.

ideas.title: Dataset biases and undesirable content
ideas.statement: Phenaki’s training datasets encode undesirable biases; the authors specifically identify violent, pornographic and gory content concerns in LAION-400M, which was included because it improved results. They report an in-training version using datasets intended to reduce such problems.
ideas.conditions: No quantitative bias or safety evaluation is supplied. Claims of minimal undesirable traits in primary corpora and mitigated future data are author-reported.

ideas.title: Models, code, data and interactive demo withheld
ideas.statement: At publication the authors choose not to release the underlying models, code, data or interactive demo because of the discussed harms and dataset issues.
ideas.conditions: Time-specific statement from arXiv v1; this extraction makes no claim about present-day availability.

ideas.title: Filtering and output-bias measurement before release
ideas.statement: The authors plan to better understand data, prompt and output filtering and explicitly measure output biases to guide mitigation through data, models or pre/post-processing.
ideas.conditions: Proposed future work, not a demonstrated mitigation.

ideas.title: Kinetics-600 tokenizer changes
ideas.statement: The Kinetics-600 tokenizer follows the BAIR setup but uses eight layers in both spatial and temporal encoders.
ideas.conditions: The inherited patch sizes are 4×4 for the first image and 2×4×4 for subsequent frames.

ideas.title: Default C-ViViT architecture hyperparameters
ideas.statement: Table 6 specifies 11×128×128×3 video dimensions, 2×8×8×3 patches after the first frame, a 6×16×16 token grid, hidden size 512, projected code dimension 32, four spatial layers, four temporal layers, MLP size 2048, and codebook size 8192.
ideas.conditions: The displayed table reuses h_z for grid height and hidden size and lists t_x=11/t_z=6, whereas §2.1 uses t_x+1/t_z+1 conventions; these table values correspond to total counts rather than directly substituting the prose symbols. B.1.1 additionally specifies eight attention heads and confirms first-frame 8×8 versus later 2×8×8 patches.

ideas.title: C-ViViT optimizer table
ideas.statement: Table 6 specifies AdamW with beta1=.9, beta2=.99, learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 1e-4, cosine decay with a 1M-step target, 100K warmup steps, clipping magnitude 10 and batch size 1028.
ideas.conditions: Batch 1028 is exactly printed. Appendix B.1.2 separately describes reconstruction-baseline training with batch 128; it is unclear whether this is a typo or a distinct configuration.

ideas.title: Main MaskGIT architecture and optimizer table
ideas.statement: Table 7 specifies sequence length 1536, 24 layers, hidden/embedding dimension 2048, MLP dimension 8192, 32 heads; AdamW with betas .9/.99, learning rate and weight decay 1e-4, cosine decay targeting 4M steps, 10K warmup, clipping 10 and batch 512.
ideas.conditions: A schedule target of 4M does not imply that the §3.1 visualization model actually trained for 4M; it is reported as 1M actual steps. B.3.1 identifies this larger architecture as 1.8B parameters and B.3.2 applies Table 7 training parameters to all text-conditioned generation.

ideas.title: Approximately 50M-parameter reconstruction encoder baselines
ideas.statement: Appendix B.1.1 describes approximately 50M-parameter encoder-decoders. The convolutional encoder has five blocks with channel multipliers [1,1,2,2,4], two residual layers and 128 hidden units per block, with embedding dimension 256. The ViT encoder uses non-overlapping 8×8 patches, eight layers, 512 hidden units, eight heads, 2048 MLP units and projected dimension 32.
ideas.conditions: Implementation used for the MiT comparison; baseline architecture details are distinct from the larger token-generation transformer.

ideas.title: Reconstruction optimizer and MiT temporal downsampling
ideas.statement: Appendix B.1.2 trains encoder-decoders and StyleGAN discriminators with batch 128, Adam betas .9/.99, linear warmup to 1e-4 over 100K steps, cosine decay over 900K more steps, and decoupled weight decay 1e-4 for both. MiT is downsampled from 25 to 6 fps and evaluated at 128×128 on 10-frame videos.
ideas.conditions: The Table 3 caption separately specifies 11 frames for C-ViViT and 10 for baseline token counts; Table 6 gives batch 1028. These source ambiguities are preserved rather than reconciled speculatively.

ideas.title: BAIR tokenizer changes
ideas.statement: For BAIR Robot Pushing, C-ViViT uses 4×4 first-frame patches and 2×4×4 subsequent patches, with eight spatial and six temporal encoder layers.
ideas.conditions: Other settings follow B.1; tokenization has finer spatial patches than the main 8×8 setup.

ideas.title: Unconditional training with frame-conditioned inference
ideas.statement: For image-conditional benchmarks, C-ViViT uses B.1 optimization without fps downsampling. MaskGIT trains unconditionally on C-ViViT tokens with Adam betas .9/.99, 10K-step warmup to 1e-4, then constant learning rate for about 2M steps; at inference, observed-frame tokens initialize future prediction.
ideas.conditions: The source cross-reference says “As described in Table 7” while discussing C-ViViT; Table 7 is actually the MaskGIT table. Dataset fps is retained for fair baseline comparison.

ideas.title: T5X text embeddings enter through cross attention
ideas.statement: For text-conditioned video generation, Phenaki uses the B.1 C-ViViT architecture/training and introduces T5X [37] embeddings via cross attention with video tokens in MaskGIT.
ideas.conditions: T5X is the pre-trained text-embedding component identified by the source; it is frozen in Figure 2.

ideas.title: Reduced 0.9B architecture for NUWA comparison
ideas.statement: For the quantitative comparison with NUWA, Phenaki uses 20 transformer layers, 1536 hidden units, 24 attention heads and 6144 MLP units, yielding about .9B parameters.
ideas.conditions: Scale matching does not eliminate differing training data or zero-shot versus fine-tuned evaluation conditions.

ideas.title: Different guidance, iteration and temperature settings by evaluation
ideas.statement: Appendix B.3 sets (guidance lambda, MaskGIT iterations, temperature) to (.1,12,4.0) for comparison against NUWA; (6,24,4.0) for image/video data-mixture ablations; and (12,48,8.0) for videos presented in the paper.
ideas.conditions: These settings are task-specific and must accompany results; do not assume the quantitative NUWA comparison used the stronger demonstration settings. Temperature semantics are not elaborated in this source.

ideas.title: Reported one-to-two-frame action response in collected data
ideas.statement: The paper reports that an action recorded at frame t is reflected in the subsequent one or two image frames.
ideas.conditions: Collection response timing claim; no distribution or independent latency measurement supplied.

ideas.title: Propagate 10Hz actions onto 30FPS video
ideas.statement: The exploration agent emits actions at 10Hz while screenshots are captured at 30Hz; for each pair of intervening frames, the preceding action is copied, yielding 30FPS action-labeled data without sending commands at 30Hz.
ideas.conditions: Timestamp alignment; the action persists for three video frames.

ideas.title: Frame-count stuttering filter
ideas.statement: Discard a video segment when its frame count f exceeds tau2, treating an excess of redundant frames and abnormally high frame count as stuttering.
ideas.conditions: tau2 and segment duration convention are not specified.

ideas.title: Autoregressive exposure bias and semantic drift
ideas.statement: Prediction conditioned on previous generated frames accumulates errors and exposure bias, potentially drifting from initial context and degrading visual quality and spatial-temporal consistency.
ideas.conditions: General motivation for a stable game-world reference, not a new theoretical bound.

ideas.title: Eight actions across diverse game scenes
ideas.statement: The dataset uses movement in four directions, jumping, swooping, and left/right view rotations across more than 90 scene styles including grasslands, castles, rainforests and valleys; later out-of-domain tests exclude these in-domain scenes.
ideas.conditions: Eight-action cardinality confirmed in Table 1.

ideas.title: Over 400 million collected frames
ideas.statement: Yan's collection pipeline produces more than 400 million image-action frames spanning more than 90 scenario styles, with 1080P resolution and 30FPS capture.
ideas.conditions: Authors' dataset description; Table 1 rounds to 400M.

ideas.title: Separate structure-dependent mechanics from appearance
ideas.statement: Yan-Edit assumes depth maps retain useful object 3D structure while discarding color/texture, enabling mechanics to be learned primarily from structure and visual appearance to be changed independently.
ideas.conditions: Design rationale for style-invariant interaction; depth-only representation need not encode all physically relevant properties, and no universal invariance proof is given.

ideas.title: Few-step DMD2 and autoregressive self-forcing
ideas.statement: DMD2 replaces pure-noise input with noisy sample data to extend one-step distillation to a few-step generator; Self Forcing generates its own training samples autoregressively to reduce accumulated teacher-forcing errors.
ideas.conditions: Cited background techniques used by Yan-Gen; effect is not separately ablated here.

ideas.title: DMD KL-gradient score approximation
ideas.statement: Equation 4 gives grad_phi L_dmd := E_t grad_phi KL(p_gen,t || p_data,t), approximately -E_t integral [s_real(u(u'_phi(epsilon),t),t) - s_fake(u(u'_phi(epsilon),t),t)] (d u'_phi(epsilon)/d phi) d epsilon. phi parameterizes causal Yan-Gen and epsilon is Gaussian noise.
ideas.conditions: Printed DMD gradient approximation follows cited DMD; u is reused in the displayed noising composition without a separate local definition, so notation is retained without inferring missing scaling terms.

ideas.title: Inject depth through copied DiT ControlNet blocks
ideas.statement: Yan-Edit's renderer injects depth maps into Yan-Gen through a ControlNet arranged like VACE: several copied DiT blocks process conditioning and add their outputs back to corresponding original blocks.
ideas.conditions: Architecture reuses ControlNet/VACE concepts; style prompts control object color and texture.

ideas.title: Depth-specific VAE and staged attention training
ideas.statement: First extract video depth with DepthFM and train a depth-specific VAE. Then train action and text cross-attention jointly, freeze text attention and fine-tune only action attention to improve consistency and fidelity.
ideas.conditions: Follows Yan-Sim's training paradigm; no numerical convergence/quality ablation for the attention schedule.

ideas.title: Random simulated depth clips for style distillation
ideas.statement: Renderer distillation uses 81-frame depth videos generated by the trained mechanics simulator with random initial depths, action signals and structure prompts.
ideas.conditions: Synthetic conditioning data from the simulator; sampling distribution not detailed.

ideas.title: Depth mechanics simulator followed by style renderer
ideas.statement: Yan-Edit disentangles interactive mechanics simulation from visual rendering: a Yan-Sim-based simulator generates depth sequences from actions and structure prompts, then a Yan-Gen-based renderer converts them to RGB under style prompts.
ideas.conditions: Two separate autoregressive components with KV caches in Figure 14.

ideas.title: Cascaded frame generation with cached history and prompt switching
ideas.statement: At inference, actions and structure prompts produce depth frames, which are rendered with style prompts; generated frame history is stored in a KV cache for subsequent generation, and users may change either prompt at any time.
ideas.conditions: Inference strategies follow Yan-Sim and Yan-Gen. The source says every generated frame is stored and claims consistency, but provides no cache size, eviction policy or long-duration memory bound.

ideas.title: Structure and style edits during interaction
ideas.statement: Yan-Edit supports text changes at any time during interaction, including structure edits such as adding interactive objects and style edits such as altering colors and textures.
ideas.conditions: Editing refers to subsequently generated interactive video content.

ideas.title: Three-category structural captions from 81-frame clips
ideas.statement: Yan-Edit segments game data into 81-frame clips and uses Qwen2.5-VL to describe 3D structure as dynamic objects, wall structures and environmental platforms.
ideas.conditions: Used for structure prompts; separate from world/local captions.

ideas.title: Structure cross-attention in depth simulator
ideas.statement: The depth simulator starts from an initial depth frame and autoregressively predicts depth conditioned on per-frame actions and a structure prompt; a text cross-attention layer is inserted after action cross-attention in every Yan-Sim attention block.
ideas.conditions: Structure prompts change geometry and interactive objects.

ideas.title: Interactive structure creation and replacement examples
ideas.statement: Yan-Edit demonstrations replace Rotate Plat with Wooden Door and Moving Wood, switch between cylinder fans, trampolines and rotating platforms, and create fans/trampolines near obstructing walls to help traversal.
ideas.conditions: Qualitative Figure 15 with action overlays; no structural-edit success rate or latency distribution.

ideas.title: Style switching at frames 81 and 162
ideas.statement: The style-edit example starts with bamboo/watercolor, changes to purple glass/cyan light at frame 81, then snow/soft pastel at frame 162; authors describe preserved mechanics while appearance changes.
ideas.conditions: Figure 16 shows selected frames through frame 242. Mechanics preservation is qualitative, with no paired error metric.

ideas.title: Mix extracted in-domain and GPT-4 open-domain styles
ideas.statement: Distillation style prompts combine style descriptions extracted from the hierarchical captions with GPT-4-generated open-domain style descriptions, intended to broaden renderer style coverage.
ideas.conditions: No prompt-generation template, style count or isolated ablation reported.

ideas.title: Reuse VACE weights before renderer distillation
ideas.statement: The authors find that combining Yan-Gen before causal post-training with released VACE ControlNet weights already provides diverse temporally consistent depth-conditioned style rendering; they therefore distill this combined model directly into a few-step causal renderer.
ideas.conditions: Avoids separately training a new noncausal depth-conditioned renderer; quality observation is not quantitatively measured.

ideas.title: Random and PPO scene exploration
ideas.statement: A scene exploration agent combines random actions with a PPO-trained RL model: random actions broaden exploration, while RL reaches positions beyond the initial region across more than 90 scenarios.
ideas.conditions: PPO implementation and exploration mixture are not fully specified; approach described as similar to PlayGen.

ideas.title: Develop human-factor and safety-aware evaluation
ideas.statement: Future work calls for richer evaluation protocols incorporating human factors and safety.
ideas.conditions: The current report mainly provides qualitative demonstrations and speed/metadata comparisons.

ideas.title: Extend prompt control into real-world domains
ideas.statement: The authors propose extending prompt controllability from the current game-based setting to real-world domains.
ideas.conditions: Future work; current action complexity remains game-bounded.

ideas.title: Scale data and models while improving efficiency
ideas.statement: Future Yan work proposes scaling the dataset and model capacity while improving efficiency.
ideas.conditions: Proposed direction, not an experimentally demonstrated scaling law.

ideas.title: Game-bounded action and interaction complexity
ideas.statement: Despite in/out-of-domain generation, Yan's action space and interaction complexity remain bounded by the underlying game, potentially limiting transfer to real-world applications.
ideas.conditions: Explicit limit on broad generalization claims.

ideas.title: Freeze appearance model while training causal action control
ideas.statement: After LoRA adaptation, drop action descriptions from the hierarchical captions and train a separate action encoder/cross-attention in every DiT block while freezing all other parameters. Frame-aligned masks enforce causal action control; 10% null-action replacement trains robustness and classifier-free guidance.
ideas.conditions: Intended to learn style-independent controls that transfer to other worlds; no isolated quantitative generalization ablation.

ideas.title: Clean-latent regression for causal initialization
ideas.statement: Equation 3 minimizes L_mse = E_{x,c_txt,c_img,c_act,t_i} ||u'({x^i_{t_i}}_{i=1}^N,{t_i}_{i=1}^N) - {x^i_0}_{i=1}^N||^2 with t_i in {T,t1,t2,0}; u' is causal Yan-Gen and N is latent length.
ideas.conditions: The displayed u' arguments omit conditions although the expectation includes them; regression targets clean latents, unlike Eq1 velocity prediction.

ideas.title: Fuse out-of-domain images with in-domain textual subjects
ideas.statement: Yan-Gen combines out-of-domain reference images with text describing an in-domain character, demonstrated by an animated husky-like subject interacting within dune, colorful-landscape and road environments.
ideas.conditions: Qualitative cross-domain fusion; no numerical generalization test. The cartoon icon in Figure 13 illustrates the textual character description.

ideas.title: Distill causal generator using frozen real and learned fake scores
ideas.statement: Yan-Gen applies distribution matching distillation to a causal few-step generator, using two score models initialized from the earlier multimodal Yan-Gen. The real score is frozen as a proxy for data distribution; the fake score continually fits current generator outputs.
ideas.conditions: Reuses DMD; 'true data distribution' is represented by a pretrained score model rather than directly known.

ideas.title: Qualitative human-controlled generation evaluation
ideas.statement: Yan-Gen evaluation illustrates text-to-world and image-to-world output through real-time human interactive gameplay, which the authors describe as having precise frame-wise action responsiveness.
ideas.conditions: No quantitative benchmark or participant/sample-count protocol reported.

ideas.title: Rectified-flow multimodal velocity loss
ideas.statement: Equation 1 defines L_fm = E_{x0,x1,c_txt,c_img,c_act,t} ||u(x_t,c_txt,c_img,c_act,t;theta) - v_t||^2, training Yan-Gen's velocity prediction conditioned on text, image and action.
ideas.conditions: Follows Rectified Flows; x_t path and v_t construction are not explicitly expanded in this source.

ideas.title: Image-conditioned classifier-free guidance
ideas.statement: For fixed-length generation, Eq2 uses u_output = u(x_t,empty,c_img,empty,t;theta) + g_uncond [u(x_t,c_txt,c_img,c_act,t;theta) - u(x_t,empty,c_img,empty,t;theta)]. The baseline retains image conditioning while dropping text and actions.
ideas.conditions: Guidance scale is named g_uncond but not numerically specified.

ideas.title: Open-domain image-conditioned interaction
ideas.statement: From reference images, Yan-Gen produces action-responsive videos in city streets, post-apocalyptic terrain, lunar scenes and canyon landscapes while retaining reference features; authors report transfer without domain-specific tuning.
ideas.conditions: Selected Figure 12 examples, not an exhaustive open-world scalability test.

ideas.title: LoRA adaptation with global-only caption dropout
ideas.statement: Fine-tune all Wan linear layers using LoRA for text-to-video and image-to-video adaptation on concatenated global and local captions. With probability 0.1 provide only the global caption to train plausible generation from sparse high-level context.
ideas.conditions: Initial distribution adaptation before adding action control; LoRA rank unspecified.

ideas.title: Claimed long interactive-video consistency
ideas.statement: The authors claim Yan-Sim can generate long interactive videos with high visual consistency throughout.
ideas.conditions: No quantitative duration-dependent error curve or tested duration is provided in this paragraph; 'infinite' elsewhere describes an autoregressive capability.

ideas.title: Text, image and action conditioning sequences
ideas.statement: Yan-Gen uses a 512-token umt5-xxl text embedding, a 257-token ViT-H-14 image embedding, and an action sequence matching video length, injected through distinct cross-attention layers.
ideas.conditions: Encoder/citation names are transcribed as printed; Figure 9 additionally shows latent tensor factors [T/4,H/8,W/8,C] and a historical KV-cache loop.

ideas.title: Causal initialization from four teacher trajectory states
ideas.statement: Following Yin et al. (2025), generate flow-matching ODE trajectories from Yuanmeng World prompts using the trained bidirectional Yan-Gen and retain {x_T,x_t1,x_t2,x_0}; replace self-attention with block-causal attention and train under diffusion forcing with independent per-frame choices among these four noise states.
ideas.conditions: x_T is pure noise, x_0 clean; called a four-step generator in the source even though listed states include the clean endpoint.

ideas.title: Continuous scene expansion after prompt changes
ideas.statement: Yan-Gen demonstrations change scene descriptions during play to extend scenes continuously, for example disco-themed to classical styling, with common tiling patterns and platform colors acting as transitions between domains.
ideas.conditions: Qualitative Figure 11; continuity is visually illustrated without an objective metric.

ideas.title: Text-to-interaction qualitative scene examples
ideas.statement: Text-guided Yan-Gen examples depict sprinting and jumping on snow, navigating a hedge maze despite foliage occlusion, moving around curtains on adobe rooftops, and stopping at greenhouse glass. Authors interpret these as physics-aligned/material-aware interactions and obstacle negotiation.
ideas.conditions: Selected qualitative samples; no measured collision, reasoning or instruction-following success rates.

ideas.title: Yan-Gen H20 throughput
ideas.statement: The distilled Yan-Gen reports 12–17FPS on one NVIDIA H20 and up to 30FPS on four H20s using unified sequence-parallel inference, supporting ongoing action input and prompt switching.
ideas.conditions: Generation resolution and detailed latency benchmark setup are not specified alongside these rates.

ideas.title: Yan-Gen four-stage causal generation pipeline
ideas.statement: Yan-Gen uses hierarchical captions, trains multimodal image/text/action conditioning, converts the model to a causal autoregressive generator using its predecessor's ODE trajectories, then self-forcing distills it for few-step real-time generation.
ideas.conditions: Addresses semantic drift, open-ended generation and latency through distinct training stages.

ideas.title: Wan multimodal video-diffusion foundation
ideas.statement: Yan-Gen builds on a pretrained Wan model with cross-attention that embeds text or image conditions.
ideas.conditions: Backbone reused for game-specific multimodal/action training.

ideas.title: Powerful-GPU dependence limits accessibility
ideas.statement: Yan's high-fidelity real-time results depend on powerful GPUs, limiting lower-resource users; efficient architectures and low-resource/edge optimization are proposed directions.
ideas.conditions: Applies to deployment accessibility, not a measured hardware lower bound.

ideas.title: Static global world caption as persistent context
ideas.statement: Generate one caption from a traversal video and hold it constant throughout a world's generation. It describes topology/region connectivity, visual theme (palette/materials/architecture), and base lighting/weather to provide an anti-drift anchor.
ideas.conditions: Authors state this prevents drift, but do not provide a quantitative caption ablation proving a guarantee. This is persistent semantic context, not an explicit token-budget compression algorithm.

ideas.title: Local dynamic-event captions
ideas.statement: For each short clip, generate a local caption describing currently visible surroundings, interactive objects whose states change, and critical events such as death or task completion to align text and video distributions for fine-grained interaction rendering.
ideas.conditions: Paired with a fixed global caption; local context changes per clip.

ideas.title: Frame-aligned interactive video data
ideas.statement: Interactive video datasets require per-frame interaction annotations explaining adjacent-frame transitions; Yan collects these in the diverse modern 3D Yuan Meng Star environment with a rich action space and complex physical behavior.
ideas.conditions: Shared training data for Yan-Sim, Yan-Gen and Yan-Edit.

ideas.title: Interactive dataset comparison
ideas.statement: Table 1 reports resolution/FPS/frame-wise/action-count/frame-scale: The Matrix 720P/60/yes/5/792M; PlayGen 128P/30/yes/5/250M; GameGenX 720P–4K/1–24/no/no action labels/192M; GameFactory 360P/16/yes/9/4M; Matrix-Game 720P/16/yes/7/50M; Yan 1080P/30/yes/8/400M.
ideas.conditions: Authors' compiled dataset metadata, not a controlled model-quality benchmark.

ideas.title: Long-horizon consistency remains unresolved
ideas.statement: Yan still struggles to ensure visual consistency over long durations, especially in complex and rapidly changing interactions, requiring spatial and temporal improvements.
ideas.conditions: Authors' explicit limitation qualifies anti-drift and infinite-consistency language elsewhere.

ideas.title: Offline video editing lacks interactive guarantees
ideas.statement: The cited diffusion video editors transform source videos with spatiotemporal coherence but assume non-interactive inputs and do not ensure edited content remains responsive to real-time user actions.
ideas.conditions: Authors' characterization of prior methods; motivates splitting mechanics from rendering.

ideas.title: Prior neural game simulation baselines
ideas.statement: MarioVGG generates Super Mario segments from text actions and an initial frame without real-time capability; the paper reports GameNGen, PlayGen and Oasis at 20 FPS in Doom, Doom/Super Mario and Minecraft respectively.
ideas.conditions: Background rates from cited prior work; the authors characterize them as lower-resolution and simpler environments than Yuan Meng Star.

ideas.title: Qualitative action-responsive movement
ideas.statement: Figure 6 illustrates Yan-Sim responding to movement, jump and sprint inputs with subsequent visual feedback, supporting the authors' qualitative motion-consistency claim.
ideas.conditions: Some frames are skipped for clarity; static samples do not quantify action accuracy or frame response latency.

ideas.title: Prior game-centric and real-world interactive models
ideas.statement: The authors distinguish game-centric models transferring action control/structural priors to open settings from real-world models predicting controlled futures; they characterize existing approaches as lacking the complete combination of real-time frame-wise responsiveness, physics, fidelity and prompt control.
ideas.conditions: Related-work characterization; not a new benchmark comparison.

ideas.title: Filter inactive or inconsistent game mechanics
ideas.statement: A rule filter removes data with inconsistent environmental interaction rules, including preparation phases where normally interactive mechanisms are inactive.
ideas.conditions: Engine-specific consistency heuristic.

ideas.title: Frame-aligned action attention and causal time attention
ideas.statement: Yan-Sim uses within-frame spatial attention, action cross-attention from an MLP-generated 768-dimensional action token tied exclusively to the matching frame, and causal 1D temporal attention allowing frame Ft to attend only F<=t.
ideas.conditions: Based on prior video-diffusion temporal attention; permits iterative generation beyond fixed-length bidirectional clips.

ideas.title: CUDA graph and compiled-kernel speed improvement
ideas.statement: Capturing the full inference pipeline in a CUDA graph removes launch overhead; Triton custom kernels optimize thread blocks and memory, with torch.compile max-autotune yielding a reported additional 1.15× speedup.
ideas.conditions: Reported engineering speed factor; detailed profiling setup not given.

ideas.title: Four-step DDIM autoregressive simulation loop
ideas.statement: Given an encoded initial frame and user action, Yan-Sim denoises a concatenated noisy next-frame latent with a four-step DDIM sampler; the decoded clean output becomes latent context for the next iteration.
ideas.conditions: Initial encoding only at startup; visual fidelity is described as satisfactory without a separate four-step quality ablation.

ideas.title: Diffusion Forcing with staged per-frame noise
ideas.statement: Yan-Sim trains its SD diffusion model using DDPM and Diffusion Forcing: add independent noise to each sampled frame latent, keep the first frame clean as ground-truth context, and stage the noise schedule so noise increases along time to match inference.
ideas.conditions: Cites Diffusion Forcing and History-guided Video Diffusion; numerical noise schedule not provided.

ideas.title: Pipeline diffusion and decoding on separate GPUs
ideas.statement: To reduce serial inference latency, Yan-Sim runs diffusion and VAE on separate GPUs and transfers generated latents through a queue.
ideas.conditions: Two-GPU deployment; GPU models for this setup are not specified here.

ideas.title: UNet pruning and FP8 speed improvement
ideas.statement: Yan-Sim structurally prunes its UNet and uses FP8 for weights and activations in all GEMM operations. Authors report 1.5–2× speedup over FP16 for FP8 operations and 1.18× overall inference speedup with minimal generation-quality loss.
ideas.conditions: No detailed pruning recipe or separate quality metrics supplied.

ideas.title: Qualitative simulation of three game mechanics
ideas.statement: Yan-Sim demonstrations reproduce acceleration/inertia on a water slide, temporary immobility after touching an electric fence, and increased jump height on a trampoline.
ideas.conditions: Selected qualitative examples rather than exhaustive physics validation.

ideas.title: Yan-Sim adapts Stable Diffusion
ideas.statement: Yan-Sim builds on Stable Diffusion using a more compressed VAE, autoregressive diffusion and lightweight/inference optimizations to target high-resolution game simulation.
ideas.conditions: Stable Diffusion is the cited foundational architecture; performance details are captured in evaluation.

ideas.title: Shift-window denoising with historical KV cache
ideas.statement: Each inference step processes a window whose earlier frames are cleaner and later frames noisier, appends a pure-noise latent and emits one clean latent for RGB decoding. Historical key/value states are cached to avoid redundant computation and reduce average latency per frame.
ideas.conditions: Pipeline amortizes multiple denoising steps across frames; history length, cache eviction and exact action-to-output latency composition are unspecified.

ideas.title: Spatial-temporal VAE compression
ideas.statement: Yan-Sim adds two single-layer encoder down blocks to raise spatial downsampling from 8 to 32 and concatenates pairs of frames along channels for temporal factor 2; the compression factors become 2×32×32 instead of 1×8×8, with 16 latent channels.
ideas.conditions: Pixel-space/latent compression, not textual prompt compression.

ideas.title: Lightweight VAE decoder
ideas.statement: Yan-Sim removes one layer from each decoder up block, adds a single-layer up block and a pixel-shuffle layer to match encoder scale, prioritizing decoder latency during generation.
ideas.conditions: Initial frames still require encoding; only decoder latency is considered in ongoing inference design.

ideas.title: VAE reconstruction training
ideas.statement: VAE training concatenates two frames into x of shape H×W×6 with H=1024 and W=1792 for the implementation labeled 1080P, and encodes z of shape h×w×16; training combines MSE and LPIPS.
ideas.conditions: Loss weights are not specified; actual training spatial shape differs from 1920×1080 capture.

ideas.title: Qualitative high-resolution diverse-scene simulation
ideas.statement: The authors describe successful high-resolution/high-FPS reproduction of diverse game styles and intricate details; Figure 5 presents a grid of rendered game scenes.
ideas.conditions: Prose says eight levels while the figure has 12 image panels; no quantitative visual-quality comparison.

ideas.title: Compiled world-simulation speed and duration comparison
ideas.statement: Table 2 reports: Matrix infinite/720p/16FPS/not low-latency; PlayGen infinite/128p/20FPS/0.05s; Genie 2 10–20s/360p/not real-time; GameFactory infinite/640p/not real-time; Matrix-Game infinite/720p/not real-time; Genie 3 few minutes/720p/24FPS/low-latency; Yan-Sim infinite/1080p/60FPS/0.11s.
ideas.conditions: Cross-paper metadata without standardized hardware or uncertainty; missing latency numbers are not zero. Yan-Sim throughput is not equivalent to 0.11s response latency.

ideas.title: Timestamp alignment of images and actions
ideas.statement: The collection pipeline records action timestamps and saves simultaneous high-resolution screenshots and action signals to form aligned image-action sequences.
ideas.conditions: Intended to learn correct responses despite engine complexity; observed response lag is separately reported.

ideas.title: Mean color variance rejection filter
ideas.statement: For frame color variances sigma_i^2, compute mean variance bar_sigma^2 = (1/n) sum_i sigma_i^2; discard the segment if bar_sigma^2 < tau1 as a rendering failure or occlusion.
ideas.conditions: Assumes failure/occlusion produces low color variance. tau1 is not numerically specified.

ideas.title: Annotated game and open-domain training data
ideas.statement: Yan combines agent-collected, cleaned game data annotated with structured captions and depth with unlabeled open-domain data for training.
ideas.conditions: Figure 2 identifies Qwen2.5-VL and DepthFM-ID as caption and depth annotators.

ideas.title: Safety-aware fine-tuning and safety tax
ideas.statement: DRESS uses natural-language feedback and other alignment datasets teach harmful-request refusal; the paper describes these parameter-changing approaches as computationally costly and potentially degrading general performance after alignment.

ideas.title: LVLM-LP first-token refusal intervention
ideas.statement: LVLM-LP applies a linear probe to first-token logits and, when a jailbreak is detected, substitutes the first token with a safe refusal template without altering the model.

ideas.title: High-sparsity safety can reflect capacity loss
ideas.statement: The authors interpret generic-prompt high-sparsity safety gains as a side effect of capacity degradation, since those masks preserve less task utility than safety-prompt masks. Section 5.4 then says the method removes safety-critical weights, conflicting with the method’s stated goal of preserving safety-sensitive weights; treat this phrase as unresolved wording, not a revised algorithm.

ideas.title: Safety prompts shift last-layer activations upward
ideas.statement: For Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct on HOD, the final-layer log-activation density shifts toward larger values after adding the safety prompt, interpreted by the authors as selective engagement of safety-responsive components.

ideas.title: HOD image calibration set
ideas.statement: The default pruning calibration randomly samples 128 images from HOD’s 10,631 images in six categories—alcohol, blood, cigarette, gun, insulting gesture, and knife—and pairs each with an image-description request.

ideas.title: Calibration equates toxic-object description with unsafe response
ideas.statement: For the HOD activation analysis, the authors treat refusal on all toxic-content image-description requests as the ideal safety behavior; Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct reportedly responds harmfully to nearly all without a safety prompt but refuses approximately 60% with it.
ideas.conditions: Final output-token activations; HOD imagery and the authors’ broad refusal policy.

ideas.conditions: Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct and LLaVA-Mistral-7B, 20%/50% sparsity.

ideas.title: JailbreakV-28K-mini benchmark
ideas.statement: JailbreakV-28K tests transfer of LLM jailbreak techniques to VLMs and contains 20,000 textual and 8,000 image jailbreak inputs. This study uses its 280-case mini version.

ideas.title: Generation preserves graph, local semantics, and attachment scope
ideas.statement: Workflow instructions must retain recovered nodes and links; semantics must stay local to the decision, validation, fallback, or termination node they govern; attachments must explicitly scope resources and checks. These are qualitative writing constraints, not a specified optimization problem.

ideas.title: LLM safety and utility evaluation protocol
ideas.statement: The extension tests Llama-2-7B-Chat and Vicuna-7B-v1.5. Hasan et al.’s safety dataset combines 225 harmful tasks (45 per category, low/medium/high severity) with ten jailbreak prompts (four role-playing, three attention-shifting, three privileged-execution) for 2,250 samples. Utility uses RTE and OpenBookQA.
ideas.conditions: The authors compare Vicuna with InstructBLIP sharing its language backbone, though LLM and VLM safety datasets differ.

ideas.title: Vicuna limits safety-pruning transfer to LLMs
ideas.statement: At 50% sparsity Llama-2 without a safety prompt reaches 91.6% DSR, exceeding dense prompted Llama-2 at 90.2%; Vicuna without prompting improves only from 5.4% to 6.3%, while prompted Vicuna falls from 13.0% dense to 8.2% pruned. The authors speculate that VLM cross-modal integration produces denser safety-critical subnetworks, but this mechanism is not established by these comparisons.

ideas.title: Magnitude pruning baseline
ideas.statement: Magnitude pruning removes weights of smallest magnitude, assuming they contribute least to performance.

ideas.title: MLLM-Protector output detector and detoxifier
ideas.statement: MLLM-Protector combines a harm detector and detoxifier in a plug-and-play system to identify and sanitize unsafe model responses.

ideas.title: MMMU utility benchmark
ideas.statement: MMMU contains college-level multimodal questions from exams, quizzes and textbooks requiring reasoning and domain knowledge across subjects and image types.

ideas.title: MM-SafetyBench scope and selected scenarios
ideas.statement: MM-SafetyBench contains 5,040 entries in 13 scenarios: 01–07 and 09 have harmful phrases; 08 and 13 cover politics; 10–12 cover legal/financial/health questions that are not inherently harmful. This study focuses on 01–07 and 09 and principally SD+Typography inputs.

ideas.title: MM-SafetyBench image formats
ideas.statement: The experiments describe Stable Diffusion images at 1024×1024, Pillow typography images at width 1024 and text-dependent height, and their SD+Typography combination; SD+Typography is the primary subset because it more effectively triggers jailbreaks.

ideas.title: MM-SafetyBench refusal-with-explanation prompt
ideas.statement: The MM-SafetyBench baseline, attributed to Liu et al. (2025b), asks the model to refuse unsafe, harmful or malicious questions and give an explanation.

ideas.title: MM-Vet utility benchmark
ideas.statement: MM-Vet evaluates integrated vision-language recognition, reasoning, language generation, OCR and mathematics abilities.

ideas.title: Evaluated VLM architectures
ideas.statement: The study evaluates Qwen2-VL-7B/2B-Instruct, LLaVA-V1.6-Mistral-7B and Vicuna-13B, and InstructBLIP-Vicuna-7B, with later scale plots also including InstructBLIP-Vicuna-13B.

ideas.title: Cross-scale safety generalization has exceptions
ideas.statement: The text attributes less stable 2B-model safety at high sparsity to limited redundancy and describes 13B baseline safety as near ceiling. Table 2 supports ceiling behavior only on FigStep/MM-SafetyBench, with dense-prompted 13B JailbreakV DSR 63.9%; Safety-Potential Pruning does not beat SparseGPT in the 2B averages (83.4 vs 83.5 at 20%,83.2 vs 86.0 at 50%).

ideas.title: Output defenses add latency and detector dependence
ideas.statement: The related work characterizes output-level defenses as effective at catching harmful content but adding latency and depending on external detector accuracy.

ideas.title: Per-output low-score pruning
ideas.statement: For sparsity s, Algorithm 1 selects low-score indices using the printed expression I = TopK(Score, s × W.shape[1]) and sets W_pruned[I] = 0. Figure 4 shows scores grouped per output neuron, pruning two of four weights in each illustrated row; its illustrative score uses S rather than the actual sqrt(S).

ideas.title: POPE hallucination benchmark
ideas.statement: POPE tests object hallucination by asking whether specified objects are present in an image, emphasizing precise visual grounding.

ideas.title: Four safety-prompt forms for pruning calibration
ideas.statement: Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct on JailbreakV-28K-mini compares a detailed refusal template with enumerated harm categories and no elaboration, a concise refusal instruction, a Self-Reminder prompt for responsible behavior, and MM-SafetyBench’s refusal-with-explanation prompt. The analysis invokes Wei et al. (2022) as an explicit-instruction hypothesis. The bibliography identifies Wei et al. (2022) as Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models; the paper supplies no direct quote substantiating the named safety-specific explicit-instruction hypothesis.

ideas.title: Prompt specificity changes the pruning benefit
ideas.statement: Figure 10 shows all four prompts improve after pruning; the detailed authors’ prompt is strongest at roughly 95% DSR at 20% sparsity and 98% at 50%, while the other prompts are roughly 92–94%. A concise prompt has the strongest unpruned striped bar (~82%) but not the strongest pruned bar. Adding a refusal explanation does not consistently improve DSR. The figure’s authors-prompt unpruned baseline (~80%) conflicts with Table 1’s 93.6% for dense Qwen2-7B on JailbreakV, with no reconciled setup difference.

ideas.title: Safety and generic prompts prune partly different weights
ideas.statement: Figure 13 shows layerwise Jaccard overlap of roughly 50–72% (prose rounds to 50–75%) between safety-prompt and generic-prompt pruned weights. Overlap is generally higher at 50% sparsity and rises again in deep layers, supporting nonidentical pruning patterns but not establishing causal safety circuits.

ideas.title: Generic pruning can damage safety circuits
ideas.statement: The related work attributes localized safety-critical neurons to Wei et al. (2024), warns that magnitude pruning can disproportionately degrade safety circuits (Hasan et al., 2024), and describes Li et al. (2025) restoring safety-relevant neurons in critical attention heads.

ideas.title: Pruning as model compression
ideas.statement: Network pruning removes redundant parameters to improve computational efficiency; this is the conventional compression role that the paper extends toward safety behavior.

ideas.title: Dense frame sampling trades detail against attention cost
ideas.statement: Dense sampling can capture subtle transitions and transient events but increases multimodal sequence length; the paper invokes quadratic self-attention cost to motivate removing redundant tokens while retaining discriminative temporal details.
ideas.conditions: Motivational complexity claim for standard Transformer attention; empirical end-to-end gains are measured separately and need not scale quadratically with kept tokens.

ideas.title: NextQA component ablation
ideas.statement: Accuracy percentages in order Cascade Plain, Seed, +Evolve, +SkillMemCat, memory-to-evolver Cat., Guide; after semicolon offline Uniform-8 Plain: Gemini [72.70,75.10,73.90,75.50,75.70,74.50;77.70]; GPT-5.2 [73.20,72.00,72.30,70.90,72.50,73.30;78.90].
ideas.conditions: Fixed VLM backbones; cascade at up to eight frames but often fewer. No uncertainty intervals reported for these table rows.

At 20% sparsity general-prompt pruning=[90.6, 85.4, 83.9, 69, 82.2], safety-prompt pruning=[92.4, 86.5, 84.3, 69.2, 83.1]; at 50% general=[100, 99.8, 68.9, 56.2, 81.2], safety=[100, 99.4, 81.4, 65.2, 86.5]. Safety prompting improves safety at 20% with similar utility. At 50%, generic prompting has equal or higher safety but larger utility loss.

ideas.title: Reported percentage gain is inconsistent with detailed table
ideas.statement: The abstract claims attack-success reductions up to 22% relative to prompting alone, and p8 says Wanda DSR is about 22% lower on both LLaVA and Qwen2 FigStep at 50% sparsity. Table 1 instead gives Safety-Potential Pruning minus Wanda DSR gaps of 32.0 percentage points for LLaVA (89.2−57.2) and 22.8 for Qwen2 (100−77.2); these comparisons use Wanda, not dense prompting alone. Retain the explicit table values rather than a single generalized 22% gain.

ideas.title: Pruning implementation and evaluation reporting limits
ideas.statement: The published method specifies channel-energy contrast, weight score and per-output illustrated pruning, but does not specify zero-score tie handling, exact pruned module selection or activation aggregation across B/L. Main safety tables report point estimates without repeated-run uncertainty; only the calibration-size ablation reports six independent runs. These omissions limit reproduction and uncertainty assessment.

ideas.title: One-shot Safety-Potential Pruning
ideas.statement: Safety-Potential Pruning removes weights unresponsive to safety prompts to reinforce safety-sensitive pathways, without retraining or architectural changes. It contrasts activations for the same query under safety and no-safety prompting and prunes low-sensitivity weights.

ideas.title: Safety prompts depend on model responsiveness
ideas.statement: Safety prompting guides behavior without changing parameters, but its efficacy depends on the model’s latent structural responsiveness to safety stimuli.

ideas.title: Safety-sensitive weight importance score
ideas.statement: Safety-Potential Pruning assigns Score_ij = |W_ij| sqrt(max(S_j,0)). Clipping makes negative-sensitivity channels score zero; the square root moderates large sensitivity values, and low-scoring weights become pruning candidates.

ideas.title: Safety Subnetwork Hypothesis
ideas.statement: The authors hypothesize that VLM safety behavior is concentrated in sparse latent pathways that respond selectively to safety prompts, especially in deeper layers, rather than being uniformly distributed.

ideas.title: Safety across model size and sparsity
ideas.statement: Figure 9 plots mean DSR across FigStep, MM-SafetyBench and JailbreakV for Qwen2-VL at 2B/7B and LLaVA/InstructBLIP at 7B/13B. Larger models often improve DSR, and 50% sparsity improves Qwen2-7B, InstructBLIP-7B and the 13B models, but not Qwen2-2B or LLaVA-7B. The plotted InstructBLIP-13B points are roughly 92% at 20% and 94% at 50%, rather than 20%-sparse 13B underperforming 7B as claimed in p9 prose.

ideas.title: Utility loss persists at 2B and 13B scales
ideas.statement: Figure 8 shows minor utility changes at 20% sparsity for Qwen2-VL-2B and LLaVA-Vicuna-13B, and larger losses at 50%. At 50% Safety-Potential Pruning gives roughly [71,58,68]% for Qwen2-2B and [55,50,63]% for LLaVA-13B on [TextVQA, RealWorldQA, ScienceQA], compared with dense roughly [80,63,78] and [66,57,72].

ideas.title: Self-Reminder prompt baseline
ideas.statement: The Self-Reminder baseline, attributed to Xie et al. (2023), asks the model to be responsible, avoid harmful or misleading content, and answer the query responsibly, without the authors’ fixed refusal template or category list.

ideas.title: SparseGPT baseline
ideas.statement: SparseGPT uses Hessian-based information to minimize performance degradation when pruning large language models.

ideas.title: Pruning and adversarial robustness
ideas.statement: Prior studies suggest pruning can improve adversarial robustness by removing features that are unnecessary for performance but vulnerable to adversarial exploitation.

ideas.title: Safety benefits are not monotonic in sparsity
