ideas.statement: Raising Safety-Potential Pruning sparsity from 20% to 50% improves Qwen2-VL-7B FigStep DSR from 92.4% to 100%, but reduces LLaVA-Mistral-7B FigStep from 99.0% to 89.2%; optimal sparsity depends on architecture, data and task.

ideas.title: WSASkill contains 70 reference skills represented by WSA
ideas.statement: WSASkill contains 70 reference skills across eight WSA types. Each reference skill is analyzed into workflow backbone, operational semantics, and attachments to define the structure and expected runtime behavior that reconstruction should preserve.

ideas.title: Calibration-aware preservation of safety pathways
ideas.statement: Future pruning strategies should explicitly identify and preserve functional safety subnetworks, accounting for calibration semantic content, prompt coverage and diversity, rather than relying only on pruning scores. The authors propose balancing specialized in-domain alignment against overfitting to narrow cues.

ideas.title: Context-dependent harms remain harder for pruning
ideas.statement: At 20% sparsity, Physical Harm DSR is 76.4% with 0.0% false unsafe and Privacy Violence DSR 77.7% with 3.2% false unsafe, suggesting genuine defense failures rather than mainly judge errors. At 50%, their DSRs improve to 98.6% and 97.8%. The authors attribute residual difficulty to subtle contextual concepts that are less easy to isolate than visible object categories such as guns or blood.

ideas.title: Vicuna-7B-v1.5 LLM safety–utility results
ideas.statement: Table 3 results (%) for Vicuna-7B-v1.5; vectors [DSR without prompt, DSR with prompt, RTE accuracy, OpenBookQA accuracy]. Dense=[5.4, 13, 63.9, 33]. At 20% sparsity, Magnitude=[5.5, 12.2, 66.1, 33.6], SparseGPT=[5.3, 14.8, 69.3, 33.6], Wanda=[5.4, 12.1, 70.3, 33.6], Safety-Potential Pruning=[5.4, 10.8, 65.3, 33.8]. At 50% sparsity, Magnitude=[3.1, 13.2, 61, 22.6], SparseGPT=[3.1, 12.9, 55.2, 30.4], Wanda=[1.7, 13.7, 55.6, 29.4], Safety-Potential Pruning=[6.3, 8.2, 63.2, 27.6].

ideas.title: Wanda activation-based one-shot pruning
ideas.statement: The paper uses Wanda (Sun et al., 2024) as a one-shot pruning comparator and explicitly builds its new sensitivity-driven metric on activation-based pruning principles.

ideas.title: Video-MME long component ablation
ideas.statement: Accuracy percentages in order Cascade Plain, Seed, +Evolve, +SkillMemCat, memory-to-evolver Cat., Guide; after semicolon offline Uniform-8 Plain: Gemini [60.33,61.56,61.33,62.78,62.56,64.22;61.44]; GPT-5.2 [55.89,54.00,52.22,54.67,52.78,55.89;58.78].
ideas.conditions: Fixed VLM backbones; cascade at up to eight frames but often fewer. No uncertainty intervals reported for these table rows.

ideas.title: Three timescales of external agent adaptation
ideas.statement: The agent state is M=(theta,S,Mv,G): frozen cloud VLM weights, a language skill library, a dense-embedding episodic store, and an edge cascade gate. G acts per frame, retrieval per question, and the evolver updates the skill bank per session.

ideas.title: Top-k prompt compression trades off accuracy by backbone
ideas.statement: Table 13 averages FullEvo across four video-QA datasets at fixed K=8 frame cap. For hot skill k=1/3/5/ALL, GPT-5.2 scores 50.48/51.90/51.47/50.12 and Gemini 3 Flash 57.27/57.73/57.49/59.43. Authors recommend k=3–5 for large or transferred banks and full injection for compact, source-aligned banks or weaker backbones.
ideas.conditions: Skill count k differs from frame cap K; no token measurements for this grid. These averages differ from headline Table 3 averages; settings are incompletely reconciled.

ideas.title: Temporally decaying scene-change thresholds
ideas.statement: The third cascade stage compares the encoded frame to a rolling reference using temporally decaying major/minor thresholds so slow scene changes or stationary cameras can eventually trigger forwarding.

ideas.title: Adaptive thresholds trade offline accuracy for reported streaming portability
ideas.statement: Despite the EgoSchema loss, authors retain temporal decay to handle slow motion, stationary cameras and irregular arrival and report a 3.4-point adaptive-over-static gain on TeleEgo.
ideas.conditions: Supplementary TeleEgo comparison reported in prose without the complete numerical profile; robustness is not fully quantified.

ideas.title: Aggregate Gemini cost reduction across four datasets
ideas.statement: Table 9 totals Full-frame/U-8+FullEvo/VisualClaw spend at $563.31/$14.19/$10.51, yielding reported aggregate savings 98.1% and 25.9%. These percentages are spend-weighted total reductions dominated by Video-MME, not arithmetic means of the four dataset percentages.
ideas.conditions: Listed dataset sizes sum to 3,323 rather than table total 3,322. Full-frame costs are approximate.

ideas.title: Concrete streaming loop thresholds and state updates
ideas.statement: Algorithm 1 discards hashes within Hamming distance six, encodes survivors and retains MAJOR frames; question handling retrieves hot/cold skills and memory with cosine at least .55, scores responses and updates hot-skill utility, buffers failures, evolves at N_evo failures, rejects names with Jaccard ≥.5, clears the buffer and lists F2 pruning every 100 questions.
ideas.conditions: F2 is optional and disabled in headline experiments. Pseudocode omits explicit buffer bounds, frame cap/silence handling and memory ingest; rolling-buffer/O(1) claims rely on prose implementation assumptions.

ideas.title: Raw memory context performs best for workspace agents
ideas.statement: VisualClaw Cat achieves 54.27% Codex macro accuracy (+2.92 versus no evolution, +4.02 versus Uniform-8) and 52.16% Claude Code (+3.16 and +8.17). Cat exceeds Guide by 0.38 and 1.39 points respectively, reversing the preference seen in most static-QA cells.

ideas.title: Claude Code Arena evolution results
ideas.conditions: Macro weights each of 200 scenarios equally; backends use different execution bridges. Cat is strongest overall; no uncertainty intervals given.

ideas.title: Codex Arena evolution results
ideas.conditions: Macro weights each of 200 scenarios equally; backends use different execution bridges. Cat is strongest overall; no uncertainty intervals given.

ideas.title: Memory-context variants on matched and broadened Arena scopes
ideas.statement: Table 15 core results: Codex ConcatMem 1860/3106 (59.88 micro,54.27 macro), related-prefix 1851 (59.59,54.02), assembled FullEvo 1848 (59.50,53.89); Claude ConcatMem 1795 (57.79,52.16), assembled FullEvo 1756 (56.54,50.77). Broader-selector Codex ConcatMem and prefix both pass 2376/3691 with 63.02/62.98 macro.
ideas.conditions: Broader 3,691-round denominator must not be mixed with the 3,106-round main table. Distinct guided variants have different macro results.

ideas.title: Cascade lowers recorded Claude Code and evolver spending
ideas.statement: Table 10 Uniform-8 versus Cascade-8 has 3,123/3,114 agent calls, 308/233 evolver calls, $665.68/$611.51 agent cost, $21.20/$15.71 evolver cost, and $686.88/$627.21 total. The total difference is $59.67. Codex evolver calls are 146/120, but provider costs are unavailable from CLI artifacts.
ideas.conditions: The printed percentage reductions use Cascade denominators: total decline relative to Uniform-8 is about 8.69%, whereas Uniform-8 is 9.51% more expensive than Cascade. Evolver-call decline is about 24.35%, not the printed 32%. Small rounding inconsistency in total cost.

ideas.title: Evolution chiefly improves hard Arena scenarios
ideas.statement: Difficulty uses average no-evolution Cascade-8 accuracy across backends: easy >75% (45), medium 55–75% (46), hard ≤55% (109). Cat versus no-evolution Codex is 86.65/86.26 easy, 65.09/65.53 medium, 36.33/30.95 hard; Claude is 83.45/84.96, 64.74/62.14, 33.94/28.61. Across backends this slightly hurts easy cases but improves hard cases from 29.78 to 35.14%.
ideas.conditions: Tiers are defined from the same baseline performance used in comparisons; mechanistic prompt-noise explanation is an author interpretation.

ideas.title: Externally scored agent workspace bridge
ideas.statement: Each step stages a clean workspace, document/data updates, image keyframes and retrieved context. Claude Code executes through a native tool loop; Codex receives a snapshot and images noninteractively and the runner applies emitted file writes after the response. External scoring checks final file state or parses MC answers and routes failures to evolution.

ideas.title: Paired text-only leakage filtering
ideas.statement: The same fixed VLM solves each scenario with and without clip frames; steps are labelled visual_required, text_only_solvable or doc_only. A candidate is retained when fewer than 40% of steps are text-solvable and clip accuracy is at least text accuracy; otherwise a single repair moves decisive clues back into visual evidence.

ideas.title: Clean-run filtering in Arena reporting
ideas.statement: All reported Codex core/ablation cells have 200/200 clean exits; Claude Code uses the latest clean per-scenario results after excluding timeout, max-turn, traceback, quota, agent-error and evolver-failure logs.
ideas.conditions: Reported task accuracy is conditioned on selected clean runs and does not quantify operational failure rates.

ideas.title: Visual-coverage and leakage-based candidate score
ideas.statement: Surviving candidates are ranked by s = v + 8 max(delta,0) - 6L + 0.5m, where v counts visually required steps, delta=Acc_clip-Acc_text is the paired accuracy difference, L is text-only leakage ratio and m counts steps requiring video plus another workspace source. The health pass requires present videos, at least 15 valid steps and a leakage label per step.

ideas.title: Arena’s expanded visual selector covers only half the scenarios
ideas.statement: All four core cells are described as complete for 200 scenarios, but the broadened video_required selector strictly covers only the 100 EgoSchema/QVHighlights scenarios; Indoor/VSI still uses an earlier narrower visual_required subset. Main results use a matched core and broadened-selector results are kept separate.

ideas.title: VisualClawArena video-grounded workspace benchmark
ideas.statement: VisualClawArena contains 200 scenarios from 100 Indoor/VSI, 50 EgoSchema and 50 QVHighlights videos, wrapping Codex and Claude Code behind a staged workspace that requires visual evidence, file editing, maintained state and executable checks.

ideas.title: Arena composition and difficulty distribution
ideas.statement: Table 2 reports 200 scenarios, 24–434 s videos, mean 24.4 steps (6.9 MC and 17.5 executable), 18.1 visual-required steps and 45/46/109 easy/medium/hard cases. VSI has 23.9 steps, 15.4 visual-required and 2/15/83 difficulty counts; EgoSchema 25.0, 21.2 and 39/10/1; QVHighlights 24.9, 20.4 and 4/21/25.
ideas.conditions: Difficulty based on average no-evolution Cascade-8 accuracy across Codex and Claude Code. Prose reports 3,106 scored steps, inconsistent with 200×24.4≈4,880; the paper does not reconcile this.

ideas.title: Within-scenario performance generally rises after an initial dip
ideas.statement: Figure 5 shows an early drop after first-step contract checks followed by generally higher later-step accuracy; VisualClaw Cat leads Codex mid/late thirds (56.19/57.38%) and all Claude thirds (52.03/50.91/53.50%). The plotted runs evolve every five day steps and include only steps supported by at least 20 scenarios.
ideas.conditions: Scenario composition varies by step; trends do not independently isolate the causal effect of adaptation.

ideas.title: Schema, modality and gold-workspace validation
ideas.statement: Arena validates schema and MC keys, timestamp citations, declared evidence modalities, and a minimum of 40% video-requiring steps; gold answers are assembled in a fresh workspace and all executable checks must pass, with malformed cases rewritten.

ideas.title: Timestamp-grounded workspace scenario construction
ideas.statement: Candidates contain a source clip, operating contract, identity and user-request cards, question JSON and executable checks, plus documents/chat/audio and dynamic updates. Gemini 3.1 Pro marks timestamps supporting visible facts, which condition newly generated steps, workspace artifacts, reference answers and scoring scripts.

ideas.title: Name deduplication and utility pruning
ideas.statement: F1 rejects proposed skills with high token-Jaccard overlap between their names and existing names. F2 logs each skill’s hit rate on scored answers and periodically prunes skills below the bank mean.
ideas.conditions: Appendix reports F2 disabled and zero F1 rejections in headline runs; activity only in supplementary longer/diverse tasks.

ideas.title: A skill bank can regress when transferred to another VLM
ideas.statement: A bank evolved to address one model’s failures can hurt another family, requiring conservative deployment defaults and model-specific bank/injection choices; performance is conditional on the target sharing the addressed failure mode.

ideas.title: Pad selected keyframes to compare at equal frame budget
ideas.statement: Cascade-fill retains all cascade-selected frames and pads to K=8 with uniformly sampled filler frames to isolate selection quality from frame count on short clips.

ideas.title: Uniform temporal coverage can beat cascade-fill on long or uniform-action clips
ideas.statement: Cascade-fill improvements are benchmark-dependent. EgoSchema distributes relevant content evenly through roughly three-minute clips, reducing scene-transition advantage; Video-MME long uses 60 s fill gaps that can miss content in static stretches. Minimum gaps are 5 s EgoSchema, 60 s V-MME, 1 s EgoPlan and NextQA, with eight-frame cap.
ideas.conditions: The appendix promises long-clip comparisons but supplies qualitative explanation rather than a corresponding numeric table; GPT-5.2 cascade-fill is unmeasured.

ideas.title: Scene-change selection beats uniform sampling at eight frames
ideas.statement: On Gemini 3 Flash at K=8, NextQA Uniform-8/cascade-fill accuracies are 77.70/79.50 without evolution and 81.20/82.70 with FullEvo; EgoPlan-Bench values are 37.96/41.54 and 50.11/52.06. Thus equal-budget cascade selection and evolution combine for a +14.10-point gain over plain Uniform-8 on EgoPlan.

ideas.title: Adaptive cascade loses offline EgoSchema accuracy at lower frame cost
ideas.statement: Table 16 on EgoSchema 200 with plain Gemini 3 Flash, seed=42 and tau_major=.20 reports uniform-8:66.0%,8 KF/Q,1,761,645 input tokens; dHash-only:57.0%,8,1,761,645; static cascade:60.5%,4.83,1,077,301; adaptive cascade:56.5%,4.83,1,083,269. Uniform beats production adaptive by 9.5 points, and static beats adaptive by four points at equal keyframes.
ideas.conditions: Ablation differs from headline threshold .30 and sample size 500. Prose calls dHash-only the worst mode, though adaptive 56.5 is numerically below its 57.0.

ideas.title: Offline video QA hides three deployment gaps
ideas.statement: Standard full-context video QA assumes all visual context is available at query time, leaves the agent scaffold fixed, and measures answer selection rather than workspace actions; live agents require unknown-length streaming, adaptation from failures, and executable task completion.

ideas.title: Retrieved stabilizing examples correct a causal answer
ideas.statement: Figure 6 Case 2 retains one of 36 NextQA frames; memories about holding a rope while descending and handlebars on trails support changing answer C moving themselves to B hold for balance.
ideas.conditions: Selected Gemini 3 Flash win; prose describes memories rerouting the evolver, while figure presents memory-bank influence.

ideas.title: A retrieved scope rule corrects a visual-purpose answer
ideas.statement: Figure 6 Case 1 keeps one MAJOR frame at about 1 s from 180 frames; precision-matching and option-elimination skills change an EgoSchema answer from picking paint to loosening color intensity, matching the purpose clause.
ideas.conditions: Selected illustrative win on Gemini 3 Flash, not an independent controlled mechanistic test.

ideas.title: A task-state rule corrects a planning action
ideas.statement: Figure 7 Case 3 retains one of fifteen frames and uses video-action-purpose-alignment and critical-action-identification-and-ranking skills to change Gemini 3 Flash’s predicted next action from (B) opening the tap to (C) closing it to complete the scissors-cleaning task with the tap already running.
ideas.conditions: Selected EgoPlan-Bench success example. The question asks for the next action given the observed progress; the skill card states that the tap is already running and the next step closes the cleanup. Panel improvement +6.18 percentage points refers to a setting-level gain, not an individual-case statistical effect.

ideas.title: Causal three-verdict streaming frame gate
ideas.statement: For each arriving frame f_t the gate uses only f_1:t. MAJOR crosses the upper threshold and uploads a keyframe; MINOR crosses only the lower threshold and updates the rolling reference without upload; SKIP does neither. Only MAJOR frames form the cloud keyframe set, allowing unknown-length streaming without future buffering or replay.

ideas.title: Approximate experiment cost and billing uncertainty
ideas.statement: Appendix A.4 estimates about $190 and 50 wall hours over roughly 50 video-QA runs with 6–12 concurrent runs. Table 14 stage runs/cost/hours are 16/$46/18, 5/$2/1, 6/$36/8, 8/~$50/~12, and 14/~$50/~10; Haiku evolver cost is bundled with Gemini accounting.
ideas.conditions: GPT-5.2 Azure-proxy reasoning tokens are not separately exposed and may inflate its cost by 1.5–3×. The stated total excludes or conflicts with much larger Arena costs in Table 10 despite prose calling it total experiments.

ideas.title: VisualClaw answer-generation policy
ideas.statement: Equation (1) generates a from pi_theta conditioned on q, G(F), Ret_S(q,k), Cat(S), and Ret_Mv(q): selected frames, retrieved hot skills, a cold catalogue and confidence-gated memory snippets.
ideas.conditions: General architecture notation; memory is routed to the evolver rather than question prompt in FullEvo.

ideas.title: EgoPlan-Bench visual-compression API cost
ideas.statement: Table 9 Gemini 3 Flash comparison: Full-frame ~23 KF/Q, ~16363 input tok/Q, $4.53/run; U-8+FullEvo 8,13348,$3.69; VisualClaw 1.13,10728,$2.97; savings 34.4% and 19.5%.
ideas.conditions: Source-reported API cost at paper-time pricing; full-frame 1 fps quantities are approximate estimates. Same evolved skill-bank configuration for cascade and Uniform-8.

ideas.title: EgoSchema visual-compression API cost
ideas.statement: Table 9 Gemini 3 Flash comparison: Full-frame ~180 KF/Q, ~192841 input tok/Q, $28.93/run; U-8+FullEvo 8,13419,$2.01; VisualClaw 2.95,9524,$1.44; reported savings 95.0% and 28.4%.
ideas.conditions: Source-reported API cost at paper-time pricing; full-frame 1 fps quantities are approximate estimates. Same evolved skill-bank configuration for cascade and Uniform-8.

ideas.title: NextQA visual-compression API cost
ideas.statement: Table 9 Gemini 3 Flash comparison: Full-frame ~30 KF/Q, ~32429 input tok/Q, $9.73/run; U-8+FullEvo 8,14025,$4.21; VisualClaw 1.51,8207,$2.47; savings 74.6% and 41.3%.
ideas.conditions: Source-reported API cost at paper-time pricing; full-frame 1 fps quantities are approximate estimates. Same evolved skill-bank configuration for cascade and Uniform-8.

ideas.title: Video-MME long visual-compression API cost
ideas.statement: Table 9 Gemini 3 Flash comparison: Full-frame ~1800 KF/Q, ~1926361 input tok/Q, $520.12/run; U-8+FullEvo 8,15818,$4.28; VisualClaw 5.41,13420,$3.63; savings 99.3% and 15.2%.
ideas.conditions: Source-reported API cost at paper-time pricing; full-frame 1 fps quantities are approximate estimates. Same evolved skill-bank configuration for cascade and Uniform-8.

ideas.title: Inherited support/query and versioning protocol
ideas.statement: VisualClaw explicitly inherits MetaClaw’s protocol structure for non-stationary task streams, including strict support/query separation and versioning, adapting it to video-QA failure distillation and using per-skill utility tracking in the role of stale-reward filtering.

ideas.title: Cascade cost is small compared with cloud latency
ideas.statement: The efficiency section reports on-device processing below 10 ms and above 100 fps CPU throughput, with cloud round trips dominating end-to-end latency.
ideas.conditions: Earlier diagram/timescale summary says approximately 10 microseconds per frame; the paper does not reconcile precision/hardware of those claims.

ideas.title: Rolling dHash deduplication
ideas.statement: The first constant-work cascade stage uses perceptual dHash and Hamming comparison against a rolling buffer to remove exact and near-exact duplicate frames such as stationary periods and camera shake.

ideas.title: EgoPlan per-skill accuracy stays near chance with sparse observations
ideas.statement: Top EgoPlan seed skills have about 27% accuracy at 225 activations each; two leading evolved skills have 204 activations at 26%; later skills have 148–188 activations at 28–29%. The paper attributes this low spread to missing visible task-progress context.
ideas.conditions: Applies to sparse cascade/per-skill diagnostics; not a universal benchmark ceiling because Table 6 reaches 52.06% with cascade-fill and FullEvo.

ideas.title: EgoSchema comparison with published baselines
ideas.statement: Table 5 lists Frozen Bilinear 17.6, LongViViT 56.8, LLoVi GPT-4o 67.6, VideoAgent 60.2, Gemini 1.5 Pro 72.2, VisualClaw streaming Guide 68.4 and VisualClaw Uniform-8 Guide 73.6 accuracy.
ideas.conditions: Baselines reproduced from cited works and use different backbones; the paper does not establish matched compute or data protocols across all entries.

ideas.title: Memory-driven personalized visual assistance
ideas.statement: The illustrative physical-world assistant retains critical frames and user preferences, retrieves skills and memories, and uses past failures to revise later answers and executable actions.
ideas.conditions: Design illustration, not a quantified deployment evaluation.

ideas.title: Frozen multimodal agent with visual and prompt compression
ideas.statement: VisualClaw combines streaming-frame cascade filtering, hot/cold top-k skill prompt injection, and memory-guided offline skill evolution; the system adapts its external scaffolding from failures while retaining frozen VLM weights.

ideas.title: Arxiv Corpus and ArxivQA split sizes
ideas.statement: Table 4 reports Arxiv Corpus train/development/test counts 2,353,924 / 3,000 / 2,500, with pre-July-2023 training texts and January–April-2024 development/test texts. ArxivQA contains 250,000 / 2,500 / 5,000 train/development/test records; its train and development contexts both come from the pre-July-2023 Arxiv Corpus train set, and test contexts come from the January–April-2024 Corpus test set.

ideas.title: Video QA experimental defaults
ideas.statement: Frozen Gemini 3 Flash and GPT-5.2 are tested using Claude Haiku 4.5 as offline evolver and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as memory encoder. Videos are sampled at 1 fps with at most eight keyframes per query; default major threshold is 0.30 with a 10 s silence ceiling, evolution after 15 failures and 12 initial skills.
ideas.conditions: The final 12-seed default appears on page 9; supplemental sweeps use other thresholds and seed counts.

ideas.title: Authors infer uneven use of compressed tokens
ideas.statement: In context-length ablations, 500xCompressor regeneration ROUGE-L F is similar for 16 and 4 compressed tokens but declines with one; similar behavior appears for QA, unlike ICAE regeneration. The authors infer that not all compressed tokens are equally used and that fewer tokens may be used more efficiently.
validity_flags: Unequal utilization is inferred from task-score curves, not directly measured per-token information content.

ideas.title: Rejection counter resets on improvement or compression
ideas.statement: Algorithm1 initializes a rejection counter, increments it on unchanged prompts, resets it upon a changed prompt, compresses and resets when it equalsK, and returns the prompt with the best validation score over the run.

ideas.title: APO CB trace degrades after an early peak
ideas.statement: The selected APO CB prompts improve from89.3 to94.6 at step1, then more specific conditionals/rhetorical examples yield92.9 at step2 and additional factual/opinion/definition rules yield91.1 at step6. Table10 says55 candidates are generated per step.

ideas.title: Fixed baseline budget may miss peak performance
ideas.statement: The authors cap baselines near300 generated prompts and observe convergence, but cannot guarantee each method’s best possible score; OPRO was originally designed for much larger budgets such as1600 prompts.

ideas.title: Concrete baseline search configurations
ideas.statement: EvoPrompt uses genetic evolution with15 initial/retained prompts,30 candidates for10 steps; OPRO generates15 candidates for20 rounds from top20 historical prompts; APO beam5 generates5 improved and6 paraphrased versions per beam prompt for6 rounds; PromptAgent uses expansion width4, depth10 and12 MCTS iterations.
ideas.conditions: Author adaptations of official code, not original default configurations.

ideas.title: Evidence is concentrated on selected base models
ideas.statement: The authors acknowledge that primarily using DeepSeek-V3-0324 may limit generalizability as model capabilities and characteristics vary; GPT-4.1 experiments supply additional evidence, while continued competitiveness on future models is a prediction.

ideas.title: Detailed DeepSeek-V3 BBH accuracy
ideas.statement: GRACE gives Geometry97.00, Translation84.29, Snarks94.74, Movie97.14, Epistemic97.50; PromptAgent gives88.50/77.86/92.63/92.63/95.50. APO ties GRACE Movie97.14, so superiority is not strict on every task.

ideas.title: Optimization on GPT-4.1 also improves BBH scores
ideas.statement: With GPT-4.1 as base, GRACE accuracy is94.50/85.00/95.79/97.14/96.50 for Geometry/Translation/Snarks/Movie/Epistemic, mean93.79. PromptAgent averages89.48, APO89.14, OPRO82.83, EvoPrompt82.55 and CoT(FS)83.50; Snarks ties APO and PromptAgent.
ideas.conditions: Separate optimization with GPT-4.1 base, distinct from cross-model transfer.

ideas.title: Biosses prompt compares concrete biomedical elements
ideas.statement: The final similarity prompt compares entities, mechanisms and outcomes: similar requires all key elements matching specificity/scope, allowing non-altering supplementary details; somewhat similar requires at least one concrete overlap with other differences; not similar means no concrete overlap despite broad themes. Output remains one of three labels.
ideas.conditions: Reported final optimizer-generated task prompt; describes the experimental artifact rather than an independently validated general rule.

ideas.title: Internal-access methods do not directly fit API-only optimization
ideas.statement: The paper motivates natural-language prompt engineering for API-based LLMs by contrasting soft-prompt training and reinforcement-learning token methods that depend on internal states or gradients.

ideas.title: Automation benefits and misuse concerns
ideas.statement: The authors suggest GRACE can reduce expert labor and manual prompt costs, while acknowledging possible misuse for tasks such as jailbreaking. They attribute this risk chiefly to the optimizer’s ability to produce unsafe content and its safeguards.

ideas.title: CB trace illustrates compression retaining score before further gains
ideas.statement: CB validation accuracy rises89.3→91.1→92.9→94.6 at steps0-3; more detailed steps4/5 score92.9/91.1 and are rejected. Step9 compresses parent3 while retaining94.6, and step13 reaches96.4 with revised general guidance.

ideas.title: CB prompt distinguishes factual negation from opinion
ideas.statement: The final CB prompt uses core meaning despite minor grammar/coreferent-pronoun differences, separates factual negation from opinion, allows implied rhetorical stance only with strong context, and avoids treating beliefs or likelihoods as factual contradictions. Output is entailment, contradiction or neutral.
ideas.conditions: Reported final optimizer-generated task prompt; describes the experimental artifact rather than an independently validated general rule.

ideas.title: Removing compression causes stagnation on TREC
ideas.statement: With compression removed, the best-validation-selected TREC test score is88.4 versus94.2 for GRACE; the uncompressed trajectory improves early then fluctuates without sustained gains.

ideas.title: Compression meta-prompt preserves core framing while simplifying
ideas.statement: The compression template asks for a self-contained compact rewrite that removes verbose, ambiguous, overly specific or non-generalizable wording, preserves core task intent, and remains easy to refine later; it requests START-tag-delimited output.
ideas.conditions: No explicit fixed token or compression-ratio target is imposed.

ideas.title: Compression merges redundancy and abstracts specific cases
ideas.statement: The compression meta-prompt both merges/removes redundant prompt elements and abstracts concrete instructions such as narrow conditionals or memorized phrasing into broadly applicable guidance.

ideas.title: K=5 balances premature compression and wasted attempts
ideas.statement: BBH tests of K=3 through7 favor a midrange threshold, with K=5 selected; small K can compress before useful refinement, while large K consumes a fixed iteration budget on stalled candidates.

ideas.title: Reported optimizer cost excludes reasoning
ideas.statement: The cost calculation uses recorded API calls and input/output tokens with published pricing, but explicitly excludes the DeepSeek-R1 reasoning process, so the reported totals do not represent complete reasoning-token cost.

ideas.title: V3-optimized prompts partially transfer to other models
ideas.statement: Without further tuning, V3-optimized GRACE prompts average85.17 on Llama3.3-70B versus zero-shot77.93 and PromptAgent80.07; on GPT-4.1 they average80.21 versus74.31 and76.74. GPT-4.1 Epistemic falls to82.50 from87.00 zero-shot, below PromptAgent84.25.

ideas.title: Default optimization budget and mixed feedback size
ideas.statement: GRACE sets T=80 iterations, three successful and three failed examples per update, and K=5 consecutive rejections before compression. Baselines are allowed approximately 300 generated prompts. The abstract describes this as25% of the prior prompt-generation budget; nominal80/300 caps are approximately26.7%, with exact compression accounting ambiguous.

ideas.title: Main evaluation uses DeepSeek-R1 optimizer and V3 base
ideas.statement: All methods use DeepSeek-R1 optimization and DeepSeek-V3-0324 as base; common Task(ZS) initialization except EvoPrompt has 14 additional variants. Candidates use held-out validation data and top-validation prompts are tested on disjoint test data, with the best test result reported.

ideas.title: EvoPrompt evolutionary baseline
ideas.statement: EvoPrompt generates candidates through genetic algorithms or differential evolution.

ideas.title: Feedback examples expose input, solution, gold label and prediction
ideas.statement: The same indexed error/correct-string template provides model input, full model response/solution, correct label and final prediction for both failed and successful examples.

ideas.title: Augment optimizer with vetted external knowledge
ideas.statement: The authors propose adding retrieval-augmented access to vetted domain repositories to help the optimizer construct useful prompts when specialized knowledge is missing.

ideas.title: Optimize task prompt within a fixed input wrapper
ideas.statement: All methods use Input=Prompt+Question+TaskSuffix+AnswerFormat. Prompt alone is optimized; suffix optionally contains answer choices and answer format supports extracting predictions. TREC example requests a boxed option.

ideas.title: Full success-count sweep peaks at three successes
ideas.statement: Figure7 extends the batch-six TREC ablation to success counts0,1,2,3,4,5 with annotated test scores87.0,89.6,91.4,94.2,91.4,90.4. Failure-heavy updates fluctuate more, while success-heavy updates can become too conservative.

ideas.title: Geometry prompt combines SVG closure, side counts and shape tolerances
ideas.statement: The generated SVG prompt counts L commands including closure, treats a globally closed path as one sequence despite intermediate M commands, and otherwise counts closed subpaths. Arcs take priority: closed arc-only paths are circle/ellipse by radii and two lines plus connecting arc define sectors. Without arcs, rectangles require four90°±5° angles and opposite sides within5%, taking priority over kites with adjacent side-pair agreement within5%; other polygons follow total sides.
ideas.conditions: Reported final optimizer-generated task prompt; describes the experimental artifact rather than an independently validated general rule.

ideas.title: GRACE alternates gated refinement and adaptive compression
ideas.statement: GRACE performs natural-language prompt optimization by filtering candidate updates through feedback regulation and validation rejection, then compressing a stagnating prompt to reopen the search trajectory.
ideas.conditions: Auxiliary optimizer LLM and task-specific training/validation examples; no guarantee of global optimality.

ideas.title: Information bottleneck motivates compression
ideas.statement: The authors relate adaptive compression to the Information Bottleneck principle of compressing input representations while preserving task-critical information, interpreting removal of redundant and case-specific content as favoring generalization.

ideas.title: Initial task instructions come from dataset and prompt repositories
ideas.statement: Methods use native task instructions where available, otherwise constructed/collected instructions from PromptSource or Natural Instructions; EvoPrompt additionally uses14 variants, paraphrased when official variants are absent.

ideas.title: Eighty iterations balance BBH performance and cost
ideas.statement: Across T=40,60,80,100,120,140, Figure 6 shows diminishing average gains after80. The authors choose80, report best results on three tasks and near-optimal on two, and suggest optional early stopping after20 stagnant steps.
ideas.conditions: Recommendation from these five BBH tasks, not a task-independent guarantee.

ideas.title: Increasing prompt length need not improve performance
ideas.statement: TREC traces show shorter compressed prompts can retain or improve validation scores; without compression, prompts continue growing while scores stagnate. The authors interpret this as accumulation of case-specific detail without general utility.

ideas.title: GRACE improves average BBH accuracy
ideas.statement: Across five BBH tasks, Table 1 gives GRACE 94.13, PromptAgent 89.42, APO 88.14, OPRO 85.51, EvoPrompt 81.15 and CoT(FS) 79.62. The paper calls the 4.7 and 14.5 improvements relative, though these closely match absolute percentage-point differences.
ideas.conditions: DeepSeek-V3-0324 base; unweighted mean of five selected BBH tasks.

ideas.title: GRACE biomedical task scores
ideas.statement: On NCBI/Biosses/MedQA, GRACE scores 73.83 F1/85.00 accuracy/86.50 accuracy, average 82.00; strongest baseline average is PromptAgent 77.60. NCBI ties APO at 73.83.

ideas.title: GRACE general NLP task scores
ideas.statement: On Subj/TREC/CB, GRACE achieves 95.70/94.20/100 accuracy, mean 96.63; APO is the strongest baseline mean at 93.94, followed by PromptAgent 92.11, OPRO 90.10 and EvoPrompt 89.00.

ideas.title: Manual task and chain-of-thought baselines
ideas.statement: Manual comparisons use zero-shot task instructions and Let’s think step by step, with few-shot variants sourced from BBH exemplars or training examples for other tasks.

ideas.title: MedQA prompt structures clinical-question reasoning
ideas.statement: The final MedQA prompt asks for systematic analysis of history, symptoms, findings and risks, prioritizing differential diagnoses using discriminating features, mechanisms and complications, while distinguishing primary causes from secondary associations.
ideas.conditions: Reported final optimizer-generated task prompt; describes the experimental artifact rather than an independently validated general rule.

ideas.title: Meta-prompt robustness tested with five paraphrases per component
ideas.statement: The authors paraphrase each update component MT,PC,FE,AG and compression component MT,AG five ways, then evaluate five BBH tasks, reporting means and95% confidence intervals.

ideas.title: Candidate generation from successes and failures
ideas.statement: At iteration t, split training samples into successes S_t and failures F_t, sample subsets, form B_t=S_t′ union F_t′, and sample candidate P_t^c from p_O(P|P_t,B_t,m1). The meta-prompt asks to fix failures while preserving effective successful patterns.

ideas.title: NCBI prompt expands disease extraction scope
ideas.statement: The final NCBI prompt extracts diagnoses, pathological states, genetic conditions, clinically established abbreviations/inheritance-pattern references, compound and multiword expressions, and clinically significant complications. Standalone genes/proteins are excluded except when integral to disease names or recognized condition shorthand; modified and unmodified pathological-state variants are included in context.
ideas.conditions: Reported final optimizer-generated task prompt; describes the experimental artifact rather than an independently validated general rule.

ideas.title: Shot coherence motivates selective compression
ideas.statement: STC assumes within-shot frames have strong visual similarity and temporal coherence, permitting removal of redundant non-keyframe tokens while preserving essential spatiotemporal cues.
ideas.conditions: Depends on reasonable shot structure and the sufficiency of retained keyframe information.

ideas.title: OPRO history-based baseline
ideas.statement: OPRO conditions prompt candidates on prior prompts and scores.

ideas.title: OPRO CB trace shows limited paraphrase gains
ideas.statement: Selected top prompts from OPRO’s15-candidate rounds mostly preserve initial meaning; validation accuracy is89.3 initially,91.1 at steps4 and16, then89.3 at step20.

ideas.title: Prompt adaptation includes discrete RL, gradient search and soft prompts
ideas.statement: Related work distinguishes reinforcement-learning editing of discrete prompts, gradient-based token optimization, learnable continuous prefix embeddings, and LLM-based closed-source prompt optimization using heuristic or error-driven expansion with search algorithms.

ideas.title: PromptAgent planning baseline
ideas.statement: PromptAgent uses Monte Carlo Tree Search and error-feedback revisions to plan prompt optimization.

ideas.title: Discrete prompt optimization objective
ideas.statement: For a base model B and question-answer task data D, select P* in prompt search space S maximizing f_B(P,D)=sum_(a_i,q_i in D) f(p_B(a_i|P,q_i)); the search space is treated as intractable to enumerate.
ideas.conditions: Initial prompt, small train/validation samples; f is a task scoring function such as accuracy.

ideas.title: Accepting every candidate reduces TREC score
ideas.statement: Removing the rejection gate and accepting all updates lowers the marked TREC test score from94.2 to88.4; compression still fires after K steps without improvement.

ideas.title: Earlier success feedback aimed at mitigating forgetting
ideas.statement: The authors acknowledge prior work [43] using success samples for avoiding forgetting, distinguishing GRACE by analyzing successes as regulation of the strength and content of failure feedback.

ideas.title: Search-based and reflection-based prompt optimization
ideas.statement: The paper distinguishes heuristic edits/paraphrases, which can stay semantically near the starting prompt, from reflection on failed training samples, which supplies stronger but potentially unstable update signals.

ideas.title: Prompt generation count is ambiguous between prose and pseudocode
ideas.statement: Appendix prose says each GRACE step produces either a candidate update or a compressed prompt and Table5 counts80 searches; Algorithm1 appears to generate an update and then additionally compress in a trigger iteration, with t=0 toT indexing.

ideas.title: Snarks prompt detects literal-contextual incongruity
ideas.statement: The final sarcasm prompt emphasizes contradiction between literal meaning and contextual intent, including exaggerated/dismissive language, rhetorical questions, implausible endorsements, falsehoods, trivialization, speaker-perspective conflict, prevailing frustrations and overhyped trends. It considers subtle intensity mismatches and contextual cues to the speaker’s true stance.
ideas.conditions: Reported final optimizer-generated task prompt; describes the experimental artifact rather than an independently validated general rule.

ideas.title: Prompt optimization cannot supply missing specialist knowledge
ideas.statement: Modest MedQA gains are attributed to examples requiring specialist knowledge absent from both optimizer and base models; the method relies on their existing capabilities and can fail on such cases.

ideas.title: Compress after K consecutive rejected candidates
ideas.statement: After K consecutive unchanged prompts/rejected candidates, GRACE samples a compressed prompt from p_O(P|P_t,m2). The compression is the new starting point for continued refinement.

ideas.title: Subj prompt separates external critique from narrative context
ideas.statement: The final Subj prompt calls author evaluations and ungrounded audience-impact claims subjective, while character perspectives, plot, genre mechanisms and internally grounded narrative descriptions are objective. Emotional/evaluative wording changes class according to narrative grounding; inherent tone/theme descriptions are subjective unless tied to specific narrative elements.
ideas.conditions: Reported final optimizer-generated task prompt; describes the experimental artifact rather than an independently validated general rule.

ideas.title: Successful examples regulate failure feedback
ideas.statement: GRACE uses known-effective patterns from successful training cases to control the content and magnitude of failure-driven candidate revisions.

ideas.title: Balanced successful and failed examples outperform extremes
ideas.statement: With total update batch six on TREC, success counts 1,3,5 yield best-validation-selected test scores 89.6,94.2,90.4 respectively. More successes generally stabilize but slow updates; failure-dominated feedback gives early gains then repeated stagnation.

ideas.title: Continuous summarization scores are mapped to success/failure tails
ideas.statement: For Reddit TIFU and Amazon Fine Food Reviews summarization, tasks use Super-NaturalInstructions prompts and ROUGE-L. The top20% of instance ROUGE-L scores are labeled correct and bottom20% incorrect to supply binary optimization feedback.
ideas.conditions: Middle60% is outside those correct/incorrect tails; exact per-task split sizes are not supplied in Table4.

ideas.title: GRACE leads ROUGE-L on two summarization datasets
Task selection and complete train-validation-test sizes
ideas.statement: The five BBH tasks were selected because DeepSeek-V3-0324 struggled with original instructions. Train/validation/test counts are Geometry150/70/200, Translation110/60/140, Snarks82/45/95, Movie110/60/140, Epistemic400/160/400, NCBI1000/500/940, Biosses60/30/40, MedQA200/100/400, Subj400/150/1000, TREC400/150/500, CB125/65/56.
ideas.conditions: Default test sets capped at1000; absent default test sets are randomly split approximately half for testing; remaining data supply nonoverlapping train/validation sets.

ideas.title: Sampling temperatures and anomalous-result reruns
ideas.statement: Optimizer temperature is0.6 and base-model temperature0. Official baseline code is adapted for budgets; experiments yielding anomalous results or significant deviations from expected performance are rerun.

ideas.title: Translation-error prompt defines a priority system
ideas.statement: The final German-English error prompt uses named entity, numerical value, modifier/adjective, negation/antonym, fact, and dropped-content categories. It prioritizes direct negation/antonyms, numbers/dates over dropped content, modifiers over facts and proper names over facts unless descriptor rules apply. Administrative type changes, color/role changes and conceptual/spatial opposites are facts; direct antonyms inside proper names remain negation/antonym errors.
ideas.conditions: Reported final optimizer-generated task prompt; describes the experimental artifact rather than an independently validated general rule.

ideas.title: TREC convergence favors GRACE at lower search size
ideas.statement: Figure 4 shows GRACE reaching 94.2 TREC accuracy within 80 candidates while baseline final scores remain at or below 90.6 after roughly 300. GRACE plotted points only mark improvements; baseline points mark optimization steps.
ideas.conditions: One task convergence illustration; plotted best test scores do not establish global optimality.

ideas.title: GRACE lowers reported TREC API cost
ideas.statement: Table3 reports base/optimizer/total USD costs and test scores: GRACE2.0/0.8/2.8,94.2; EvoPrompt6.5/0.5/7.0,85.4; OPRO7.3/1.3/8.6,86.4; APO2.0/1.6/3.6,90.6; PromptAgent6.6/3.9/10.5,90.2.
ideas.conditions: TREC run and model/API prices used in paper; not current pricing.

ideas.title: TREC prompt classifies the required answer rather than question topic
ideas.statement: The final prompt defines six answer types: abbreviation, entity, description/concept, human including organizations, location including nationality/URLs, and standalone numeric values. It prioritizes descriptions over named humans unless a name is required, terms/lists as entities, explanations as concepts, and entity-associated numerical attributes under the entity’s category rather than numeric. It includes explicit borderline examples.
ideas.conditions: Reported final optimizer-generated task prompt; describes the experimental artifact rather than an independently validated general rule.

ideas.title: Detailed TREC API calls and input/output tokens
ideas.statement: Table11 gives base API/input/output and optimizer API/input/output respectively: EvoPrompt45K/3.8M/5.4M and318/0.1M/0.2M; OPRO45K/6.9M/5.7M and300/0.4M/0.5M; APO9.7K/5.6M/1.0M and574/0.6M/0.6M; PromptAgent33.6K/24.3M/2.7M and448/3.0M/1.1M; GRACE14.4K/6.9M/0.9M and80/0.3M/0.3M.
ideas.conditions: Counts for one TREC optimization run; K/M are thousands/millions.

ideas.title: Failure-only feedback can overcorrect prompts
ideas.statement: The authors argue that aggressive biased error feedback can cause prompt overcorrection and semantic drift; case-specific prompt enrichment can plateau through poor generalization.

ideas.title: Update meta-prompt enforces preservation and generalizable edits
ideas.statement: The update template embeds the current prompt plus successes and failures, asks to preserve correct answers and solutions, fix errors with coherent generalizable instructions, avoid special-case logic/examples, keep changes minimal and stable, leave wrappers/verbalizers fixed, and output within START tags.
ideas.conditions: Instructional intent of the optimizer template, not a guarantee that generated prompts obey it.

ideas.title: Update-meta-prompt paraphrases preserve BBH performance
ideas.statement: Five paraphrases per component produce BBH averages94.04 MT,94.09 PC,93.95 FE and93.92 AG versus original94.13. Reported per-task95% interval quantities range0.29-1.60 points across these update variants.

ideas.title: BEATs balances recall and precision in audio-only augmentation
ideas.statement: Without shot-aware compression, Table VI reports QVHighlights [R1@0.5,R1@0.7,mAP@0.5,mAP@0.75]: BEATs [77.23,64.52,70.02,56.66], Whisper [77.16,62.71,68.89,55.33], Encodec [77.68,63.10,68.19,54.51].
ideas.conditions: BEATs wins three metrics; Encodec has higher R1@0.5. This ablation excludes other additions such as STC and is not the full SMART result.

ideas.title: BEATs audio encoding with temporal pooling
ideas.statement: SMART extracts raw audio, resamples it to 16 kHz, encodes it with pretrained BEATs, temporally average-pools the features, and projects them to the multimodal language-model feature space.
ideas.conditions: Audio compression trades acoustic detail for sequence efficiency; main-text [1] citation numbering is inconsistent with the main bibliography, but appendix A/reference [1] identifies BEATs.

ideas.title: Global concatenation outperforms explicit fusion in most metrics
ideas.statement: QVHighlights Table V [R1@0.5,R1@0.7,mAP@0.5,mAP@0.75] reports Overall Concatenation [77.23,64.52,70.02,56.66], Audio-Visual Fusion [24.84,16.23,20.47,12.26], Interleaved Alignment [76.71,63.16,70.01,56.12], and Voice + Ambient Sound [76.00,63.61,69.82,56.83].
ideas.conditions: Global concatenation wins three metrics, while Voice + Ambient Sound wins mAP@0.75. Limited-data optimization and disrupted global context are proposed explanations; detailed fusion architectures are unspecified.

ideas.title: Average audio pooling wins three metrics while attention wins stricter mAP
ideas.conditions: Average is the adopted default for performance and simplicity. Prose calls max pooling worst overall, but attention is lower than max on three of four metrics; noise-overemphasis explanation is conjectural.

ideas.title: Qualitative separation of beach speech moments
ideas.statement: For a man talking from a beach, ground truth is 52–88 and 96–98 s; visual-text MLLM predicts 50–98 s and SMART predicts 52–88 and 90–98 s.
ideas.conditions: Audio is proposed to help identify the speech gap, but SMART still starts the second interval six seconds early.

ideas.title: Coarse audio shifts and shuffling cause modest performance losses
ideas.conditions: Losses are 0.71–0.91 recall points and 0.47–0.60 mAP points across tested perturbations; supports coarse-context robustness, not precise synchronization capability. Chunk length and edge handling are not detailed.

ideas.title: Audio and STC provide complementary ablation gains
ideas.conditions: Combined gains over this ablation baseline are [2.13,1.80,1.47,1.47] percentage points; baseline differs from the named LLaVA-MR Table I row.

ideas.title: Global audio compression may lose event timing
ideas.statement: Because SMART compresses global audio context rather than explicitly modeling fine-grained audio-visual alignment, it may miss subtle acoustic-event timing in complex scenes.
ideas.conditions: Acknowledged limitation; retained order does not guarantee precise temporal grounding.

ideas.title: Evaluation requires raw audiovisual inputs
ideas.statement: The authors omit ActivityNet Captions because their commonly used official video release is silent, and omit TACoS and MAD because commonly provided pre-extracted visual features lack raw frames or audio needed for shot detection and encoding.
ideas.conditions: The exclusion rationale concerns the supplied data releases and full SMART pipeline; it does not establish that all possible versions of these datasets lack audio.

ideas.title: Charades-STA test performance
ideas.statement: SMART reports mIoU 61.09, R1@0.5 72.26, R1@0.7 52.17, mAP@0.5 69.47 and mAP@0.75 40.43; LLaVA-MR reports 59.78, 70.65, 49.58, 69.96 and 39.66. SMART improves recall by 1.61 and 2.59 percentage points but has lower mAP@0.5.
ideas.conditions: Reported Charades-STA test comparison; Mr.BLIP mIoU is 58.63, so prose calling it the previous best overlooks Table I’s LLaVA-MR mIoU of 59.78.

ideas.title: Keyframe selection and filtering transfer to Video-LLaMA
ideas.statement: Adding keyframe selection and non-keyframe token filtering to Video-LLaMA raises Charades-STA R1@0.5 from 48.93 to 53.26, R1@0.7 from 27.64 to 30.12, and mIoU from 31.27 to 32.94.
ideas.conditions: Video-LLaMA already includes audio, so no new audio branch is added. This is transfer of visual compression components, not a fully identical SMART pipeline or broad backbone generalization proof.

ideas.title: Distribution shifts and open-world behavior remain unestablished
ideas.statement: Moderate boundary-perturbation robustness and one backbone transfer experiment do not establish behavior under larger distribution shifts or broad open-world settings.
ideas.conditions: The paper explicitly identifies these as remaining work.

ideas.title: Cooking failure confuses visually distinct stages
ideas.statement: For adding flour and stock to a pan, Figure 10 example 2 shows baseline matching ground truth from video start to 28 s, while SMART predicts 74–88 s.
ideas.conditions: Authors hypothesize similar kitchen sounds attract a later semantically related step; no isolated audio intervention verifies the cause.

ideas.title: Eating-fish failure selects a much later interval
ideas.statement: For a man in a pink top eating fish, Figure 10 example 3 ground truth is 54–70 s, baseline predicts 56–68 s, and SMART predicts 132–148 s.
ideas.conditions: A vision-sufficient query with allegedly unhelpful soundtrack; repeated semantics/audio interference are proposed explanations.

ideas.title: Glass-building failure favors an incorrect earlier moment
ideas.statement: Figure 10 example 1 ground truth is 124–140 s and SMART predicts 70–82 s. The visual-text baseline figure shows both 84–100 and 124–140 s.
ideas.conditions: The prose mentions only baseline 84–100 s and omits its plotted correct interval. The proposed irrelevant-audio explanation remains a hypothesis.

ideas.title: Lightweight repair of generated intervals
ideas.statement: SMART applies lightweight post-processing heuristics to correct minor formatting inconsistencies in language-model outputs.
ideas.conditions: The paper does not give the exact heuristics, so their effects on prediction validity cannot be independently reconstructed from this description.

ideas.title: 80 frames and 32 keyframes balance coverage and compression
ideas.statement: Figure 6 reports the best QVHighlights STC configuration at N=80 sampled frames and k=32 keyframes.
ideas.conditions: Displayed comparisons combine N and k changes; the finite sweep does not establish a universal optimum. Too few keyframes may overcompress and too many may restore redundancy.

ideas.title: Audio serves as context without explicit alignment
ideas.statement: SMART uses temporally ordered BEATs acoustic features and positional embeddings as complementary global audio context rather than inserting timestamps or explicitly enforcing fine-grained audio-visual alignment.
ideas.conditions: This design may miss fine audio-event timing despite preserving feature order.

ideas.title: Global-local representation design is an analogy for SMART
ideas.statement: The authors relate ActBERT’s combination of global action information and local object regions to SMART’s goal of preserving coarse temporal organization while reducing local redundancy.
ideas.conditions: The paper explicitly says ActBERT predates recent MLLMs and does not address audio-enhanced moment retrieval; conceptual analogy does not establish adopted implementation.

ideas.title: Weakly relevant audio can mislead visual grounding
ideas.statement: SMART can perform worse than a visual-text baseline when a primarily visual query is paired with irrelevant, ambiguous or weakly related audio context.
ideas.conditions: Failure examples suggest interference but do not isolate the audio branch from STC or other full-model differences.

ideas.title: Keyframe selection follows high dynamics in an example
ideas.statement: Figure 7 plots frame-dynamic scores across about 80 sampled positions and marks selected high-score keyframes; selected frames remain full visual observations while non-keyframes enter token filtering.
ideas.conditions: Illustrative QVHighlights basketball-family example, not quantitative validation of spatial semantic fidelity.

ideas.title: Dense video tokens constrain temporal context
ideas.statement: Long visual input sequences raise memory and computational demands and restrict the video context that language models can process.
ideas.conditions: Motivation for compression rather than a formal lower bound on retrieval performance.

ideas.title: Multimodal adapters bridge vision and language
ideas.statement: Related work describes gated cross-attention, adapters, projection layers and Q-Formers as mechanisms for bridging visual and text representations, with video adaptations adding temporal inputs and retrieval-oriented models improving semantic alignment.
ideas.conditions: The paragraph provides a family-level literature summary, not comparative experimental proof across the cited models.

ideas.title: Nested start-end interval generation
ideas.statement: Following Mr. BLIP, SMART prompts the language model to generate one or more moments as a nested list of start and end timestamps in seconds.
ideas.conditions: Example output format [[s1,e1],[s2,e2],…].

ideas.title: Visual timestamps followed by global audio context
ideas.statement: The language-model input is x=[t1,v1L,t2,v2L,…,VE,a1L,a2L,…,AE,q,p], with a timestamp before each visual frame embedding, end-of-modality separators, and then query and prompt.
ideas.conditions: Audio tokens have no explicit individual timestamp alignment to visual frames; notation uses viL for frame-associated visual tokens.

ideas.title: LoRA adaptation and optimization schedule
ideas.statement: SMART fine-tunes 0.63% of model parameters with LoRA, uses AdamW with learning rate warmed from 1e-8 to 3e-4 over the first 10% of iterations and cosine decay thereafter, and samples frames randomly during training.
ideas.conditions: Reported implementation; exact base language-model identity, LoRA rank and formatting heuristics are not specified in this passage.

ideas.title: STC contrasts shot-aware selection with pooling and clustering
ideas.statement: The paper contrasts STC with CenterCLIP token clustering and prior token pooling, arguing these can lose fine dynamic detail while shot-local redundancy reduction preserves temporal coherence.
ideas.conditions: This passage is qualitative motivation; Table VIII empirically compares average pooling, not every cited compression algorithm.

ideas.title: Prompt refinement lacks a complete reproducible template
ideas.statement: The paper claims a refined audio-visual prompting strategy and specifies the multimodal token order plus nested timestamp output format, but does not supply a complete textual prompt template in the audited 14 pages.
ideas.conditions: Extraction-level assessment of reproducibility based on full-source audit; no invented prompt wording.

ideas.title: Chair example shows recovery with temporal overextension
ideas.statement: Figure 9 example 3 ground truth is 2–20 and 30–32 s; baseline predicts 0–20 s and SMART predicts 2–20 and 28–32 s.
ideas.conditions: SMART recovers the late chair-leaning event but starts it two seconds early; narrative audio-cue attribution is not experimentally isolated.

ideas.title: Qualitative recovery of disjoint earplug-sharing intervals
ideas.statement: In Figure 4’s earplug-sharing example, the visual-text MLLM predicts the whole 0–150 s clip; SMART predicts 48–82, 96–128 and 138–150 s against ground truth 58–82, 96–106, 124–128 and 138–150 s.
ideas.conditions: Illustrative case; SMART still extends boundaries and merges two disjoint moments. Attribution of gains to dialogue and compression is explanatory speculation, not an isolated causal test.

ideas.title: Additional outfit example recovers a short later moment
ideas.statement: Figure 9 example 1 ground truth is 0–18 and 26–28 s, visual-text MLLM predicts only 0–18 s, and SMART predicts 0–20 and 26–28 s.
ideas.conditions: Selected QVHighlights example; SMART recovers the late interval but slightly overextends the first. Audio narration/ambient explanations are speculative.

ideas.title: Qualitative localization with named-location audio
ideas.statement: In the Armenia protest example, ground truth has 28–38, 62–72 and 140–150 s; the baseline misses the middle interval, while SMART retrieves 28–38, 62–72 and 142–150 s. The authors attribute the middle recovery to reporter speech naming Armenia.
ideas.conditions: Selected example; the asserted spoken cue is reported by authors rather than independently verified from an audio track in the PDF.

ideas.title: Tower example improves missing initial moment but overextends the long one
ideas.statement: Figure 9 example 4 ground truth is 8–10 and 14–118 s; the baseline visually matches the long 14–118 s interval but misses 8–10 s; SMART predicts 8–10 and 12–120 s.
ideas.conditions: The prose says the baseline truncates/misses part of the long second interval, contrary to its plotted labels. Preserve plotted intervals and flag the discrepancy.

ideas.title: Qualitative trail-walking localization
ideas.statement: For two men walking down a trail, Figure 4 shows ground truth 92–106 s, visual-text predictions 78–82 and 94–106 s, and SMART 92–106 s.
ideas.conditions: Selected example; prose mentions the erroneous interval while the figure also displays the partly correct baseline interval.

ideas.title: QVHighlights queries mostly need vision alone
ideas.statement: The paper categorizes QVHighlights queries as 74.71% vision-sufficient, 22.00% audio-helpful and 3.29% audio-dependent.
ideas.conditions: Classification protocol, annotation agreement and exact denominator are not provided in this analysis; proportions characterize the reported grouping.

ideas.title: Audio-relevant query groups show the largest SMART gains
ideas.statement: Table IX reports baseline→SMART R1@0.5 and mAP@0.5: audio-dependent 58.82→67.65 and 61.76→68.14; audio-helpful 68.55→73.27 and 62.30→65.36; vision-sufficient 79.73→80.18 and 70.17→71.64.
ideas.conditions: QVHighlights reported breakdown; gains are +8.83/+6.38, +4.72/+3.06 and +0.45/+1.47 points. Full SMART also includes STC, so the table alone does not isolate audio causally.

ideas.title: QVHighlights test performance
ideas.statement: SMART reports R1@0.5 78.15, R1@0.7 63.16, mAP@0.5 70.76 and mAP@0.75 55.54. LLaVA-MR reports 76.59, 61.48, 69.41 and 54.40; Mr.BLIP reports 74.77, 60.51, 68.12 and 53.38. FlashVTG mAP@0.5 is 72.33, above SMART.
ideas.conditions: QVHighlights test set; +1.56 and +1.68 percentage points in recall versus LLaVA-MR. Table contradicts blanket best-across-major-metrics wording.

ideas.title: QVHighlights validation performance
ideas.statement: Table I reports SMART mIoU 72.03, R1@0.5 78.65, R1@0.7 65.03, mAP@0.5 70.46 and mAP@0.75 56.72. LLaVA-MR reports 71.85, 78.13, 64.13, 69.64 and 56.32 respectively. FlashVTG has higher mAP@0.5 at 72.75.
ideas.conditions: Differences versus LLaVA-MR are percentage points, including +0.52 R1@0.5 and +0.90 R1@0.7. No uncertainty or repeated-run tests are reported in Table I.

ideas.title: Compression may reduce reliance on redundant evidence
ideas.statement: SMART motivates shot-aware compression as a way to reduce repeated visual evidence and focus on temporally informative content.
ideas.conditions: The paper does not directly target dataset debiasing; strong in-distribution performance is not proof of robust temporal understanding.

ideas.title: Temporal retrieval metrics
ideas.statement: R1@0.5 and R1@0.7 assess top-one temporal localization at specified IoU thresholds; mIoU summarizes segment overlap and mAP reports localization precision.
ideas.conditions: The source describes standard retrieval metrics, but does not fully specify benchmark aggregation or matching code.

ideas.title: TransNetV2 establishes compression units
ideas.statement: SMART first divides videos into shots with TransNetV2, using learned visual transition cues to guide intra-shot compression.
ideas.conditions: Shot segmentation is a preprocessing dependency; robustness is later evaluated under perturbations.

ideas.title: STC tolerates moderate boundary errors
ideas.statement: Table X reports QVHighlights [R1@0.5,mAP@0.5]: TransNetV2 [78.65,70.46], fixed-length pseudo-shots [77.74,69.95], ±5-frame boundary perturbation [78.00,69.96], 20% boundary merge/drop corruption [77.81,70.03].
ideas.conditions: Reasonable shot boundaries help, but perfect segmentation is unnecessary in these tests. Fixed shot length, perturbation sampling and merge/drop mixture are not specified; results do not cover arbitrary segmentation failure.

ideas.title: SMART audio-enhanced shot-aware retrieval
ideas.statement: SMART combines a pretrained multimodal language model, visual and audio encoders, and shot-aware visual token compression to predict query-relevant video intervals.
ideas.conditions: The architecture uses frozen encoders and a LoRA-tuned language model; claimed benefits require empirical qualification.

ideas.title: Token filtering alone is faster but less accurate
ideas.statement: Table IV reports keyframe only 88.75% tokens, 21.29 GB, 2368.54 ms, 0.4456 samples/s; filtering only 56.00%, 19.42 GB, 2168.47 ms, 0.4924 samples/s. Filtering alone is more efficient than full SMART but underperforms it on all four Table III retrieval metrics.
ideas.conditions: QVHighlights, reported stage variants; efficiency and retrieval must be considered together.

ideas.title: STC reduces tokens, peak memory and inference latency
ideas.statement: Table IV on QVHighlights reports baseline with audio token retention 100%, memory 21.94 GB, latency 2451.49 ms and throughput 0.4331 samples/s; SMART retains 78.89%, uses 20.72 GB, takes 2224.04 ms and reaches 0.4750 samples/s.
ideas.conditions: Reported end-to-end measurements; Table IV does not fully specify measurement repetitions or timing boundaries. Lower retained-token fraction produces smaller memory and latency reductions than its raw token savings.

ideas.title: Preserve keyframes and compress non-keyframes
ideas.statement: Shot-aware Token Compression preserves representative keyframes as complete frames while retaining high-temporal-variance query tokens and discarding low-variance tokens only from non-keyframes.
ideas.conditions: Two-stage shot-aware design; low-variance information is expected to remain represented in keyframes.

ideas.title: Gaussian-smoothed feature changes select keyframes
ideas.statement: STC computes patch-wise changes between consecutive image-encoder frame features, takes each difference vector’s L2 norm to obtain a motion-magnitude sequence, Gaussian-smooths it, and chooses high-magnitude frames as keyframes.
ideas.conditions: Higher smoothed change is treated as informative dynamics; exact Gaussian bandwidth and selection tie rules are not supplied in this description.

ideas.title: Temporal variance at Q-Former query positions filters tokens
ideas.statement: For each shot, STC computes temporal variance at each of Q Q-Former query positions. It retains high-variance tokens across frames and removes low-variance tokens only from non-keyframes, whose redundant content is expected to be inferable from corresponding keyframe tokens.
ideas.conditions: Main prose calls the score temporal variance; Figure 8 specifies mean temporal standard deviation of Q-Former query features after T5 projection. Exact retention threshold or ratio-selection rule is not given.

ideas.title: VMR evolved from window matching to direct boundaries and alignment
ideas.statement: The related-work section describes TALL sliding-window query matching, attention-based direct temporal boundary prediction, semantic-conditioned dynamic modulation, and Moment Alignment Network structured reasoning as prior visual-text approaches.
ideas.conditions: Source-authored overview, with frame-supervised and zero-shot methods as later settings; these are background comparisons, not SMART components.

ideas.title: Combined STC stages improve most retrieval metrics
ideas.statement: QVHighlights Table III reports [R1@0.5,R1@0.7,mAP@0.5,mAP@0.75]: keyframe only [77.35,63.81,69.95,56.76], token filtering only [76.90,64.19,69.21,55.94], full SMART [78.65,65.03,70.46,56.72].
ideas.conditions: Compared with Table II audio-only [77.23,64.52,70.02,56.66], token filtering alone lowers all four values; keyframe-only wins mAP@0.75 by 0.04 over SMART. Full SMART is best in three of four stage-wise metrics.

ideas.title: Mean temporal standard deviation ranks projected tokens
ideas.statement: The Figure 8 caption defines actual intra-shot filtering score s(q)=(1/D) sum from d=1 to D of Std over t in S of h[t,q,d], computed within shot S on Q-Former visual query tokens after T5 projection; tokens with highest scores are retained.
ideas.conditions: The earlier method prose says variance, but the caption explicitly uses standard deviation. Highest-score retention does not specify a numerical cutoff.

ideas.title: Encoder patch difference heatmaps visualize dynamics
ideas.statement: Figure 8 computes H_t(p)=||z[t,p]−z[t−1,p]||2 from LayerNorm-normalized visual-encoder patch features, excluding any CLS token before spatial reshaping. Warmer colors indicate larger adjacent-frame change.
ideas.conditions: These are temporal-dynamics visualizations, not attention maps or the actual Q-Former token-retention score.

ideas.title: Dataset-specific sampling and training compute
ideas.statement: Charades-STA training uses 60 frames/video, 30 epochs, batch size 16 and four GPUs; QVHighlights uses 80 frames/video, 30 epochs, batch size 32, eight GPUs and gradient accumulation factor 4. Experiments use 80 GB NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
ideas.conditions: Paper-reported setup; batch-size interpretation with accumulation is not further detailed.

ideas.title: Shot-aware compression outperforms uniform pooling
ideas.statement: On Charades-STA, Table VIII [R1@0.5,R1@0.7,mIoU] reports no compression [68.52,47.29,58.16], average pooling [69.43,48.17,58.77], and proposed shot-aware compression [70.39,49.03,59.47].
ideas.conditions: This comparison differs from the full SMART Table I setting/results; supports benefit of preserving full keyframes and filtering non-keyframes, with unspecified matching of compression budgets.

ideas.title: Aggressive visual compression may weaken fine details
ideas.statement: Even with intact keyframes, aggressive non-keyframe compression or highly dynamic motion can weaken subtle visual evidence.
ideas.conditions: Acknowledged limitation of variance-based compression.

ideas.title: EVA-CLIP and Q-Former visual representation
ideas.statement: Sampled frames are encoded by EVA-CLIP into N×P×Dv image embeddings; Q-Former maps each frame to Q query features in Dq dimensions, which are projected to the LLM space before token compression.
ideas.conditions: Compressed visual output has Sv tokens of dimension DL.

ideas.title: Compression ratio is retained token fraction
ideas.statement: For compressed prompt xhat, alpha=L_xhat/L_x in [0,1], where alpha=1 means no compression and smaller alpha means stronger compression (equation 3). A k× reduction corresponds to retained fraction 1/k.

ideas.title: Paper does not specify key replay and reconstruction implementation details
ideas.statement: Within the ten-page paper, the experimental description does not identify the generator/replay model, prompts, decoding parameters, exact fidelity scoring rule or judge, run counts, train/test separation, per-type counts, baseline version, or statistical uncertainty. These omissions limit independent interpretation and reproduction from the paper alone.
ideas.conditions: Extractor assessment of the complete paper; linked code/supplements may provide further information but were not evaluated here.

ideas.title: Constrained generation preserves evidence, rare paths, and uncertainty
ideas.statement: Generated skills include activation conditions, workflow, decision-node semantics, attachments, validation, and output behavior. Every major instruction must be traceable to W/S/A evidence; alternative and rare paths remain explicit; missing tool arguments, failure modes, or branch conditions are marked unobserved or trigger clarification instead of invented rules.

ideas.title: Attachments combine skill-wide and node-local bindings
ideas.statement: Equation 6 writes Â = Â_global ∪ Â_node. Global attachments define the environment; local attachments bind resources, actions, checks, or output obligations to one execution unit. WSA decomposition allows missing nodes, wrong links, wrong functions, and mis-scoped attachments to be distinguished.

ideas.title: Introduction claims broader consistency than the detailed evidence establishes
ideas.statement: The introduction claims consistent W2S superiority over Anthropic Skill Creator on both structural fidelity and behavioral consistency under equal interaction evidence; the detailed experiment reports a single behavioral metric and a T5 exception.
ideas.conditions: Extractor cross-section observation; Table 3 and Section 6 qualify the introduction claim.

ideas.title: S maps recovered nodes to goals, criteria, outcome, and quality
ideas.statement: Equation 5 schematically writes Ŝ: N̂ → {goal, criteria, outcome, quality}. It scopes goals, decision criteria, validation rules, examples, and outcomes to the node where they affect behavior; it is explicitly not a fixed schema.

ideas.title: Operational semantics attach meaning and criteria to nodes
ideas.statement: S records each relevant node’s local objective, decision logic, execution conditions, and success/failure criteria, assigning executable meaning to workflow units.

ideas.title: Programmatic agent skills support execution-based verification
ideas.statement: The cited Agent Skill Induction work represents induced skills as executable programs, enabling correctness verification through execution rather than only free-form lessons.

ideas.title: Skill consists of routing plus WSA runtime specification
ideas.statement: Equation 1 writes Skill = (R, W + S + A), where R governs selection, W encodes the execution skeleton and dependencies, S specifies node interpretation/execution, and A defines tools, resources, constraints, state operations, validation, and output schemas. The plus signs denote a conceptual decomposition rather than defined numerical addition.
ideas.conditions: Representational formalism, not an optimization objective or proved theorem.

ideas.title: Skill-IR decomposes executable skills into WSA
ideas.statement: Skill-IR represents workflow structure, execution semantics, and runtime attachments as complementary structural, behavioral, and operational components, covering task decomposition, step requirements, control-flow conditions, verification, and safety-critical state management.

ideas.title: SkillRL co-evolves a hierarchical skill library with policy
ideas.statement: SkillRL distills trajectories into a hierarchical skill library that co-evolves with the agent policy during reinforcement learning.

ideas.title: Agent skill as a reusable runtime specification
ideas.statement: A skill packages a reusable agent capability and specifies when to activate it and how to use it across future tasks.

ideas.title: Skills are explicit procedural memory artifacts
ideas.statement: Skills encode reusable composition of primitive capabilities and serve as editable, versionable, portable, and auditable procedural memory across tasks and compatible runtimes.

ideas.title: How to improve resource and constraint scoping in attachment-heavy workflows
ideas.statement: The authors propose stronger mechanisms for scoping runtime resources and constraints in future W2S versions to address attachment-heavy workflow failures.
ideas.conditions: Motivated by T5 underperformance; no concrete follow-up mechanism or evaluation is given.

ideas.title: Branch, loop, approval, fallback, and termination functions belong in S
ideas.statement: W2S reconstructs W as execution units and directed links only. Branching, looping, approval, fallback, and termination are node functions in S rather than separate W elements. For a one-unit reference skill, reconstruction yields one node and no edges and generation skips workflow instructions.
ideas.conditions: Examples of execution units are intake, retrieval, filtering, planning, checking, and response generation.

ideas.title: Skill utility depends on preserving runtime structure
ideas.statement: W2S builds on the perspective that control logic, node-local semantics, and runtime attachments jointly govern future behavior. Losing activation, branch, retry, fallback, tool-use, validation, or termination conditions can change execution despite preserving salient text.
ideas.conditions: Conceptual dependence on the cited runtime-structure perspective; no claim of implementing SSL. Liang et al. title/authors and pre-June chronology verified from primary arXiv metadata https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24026; bibliography prints arXiv:2604.24026.

ideas.title: W2S underperforms ASC on workflow-plus-attachment skills without explicit semantics
ideas.statement: T5 combines W+A without S and is the sole negative W2S–ASC gap (0.480 versus 0.550). The authors attribute this to difficulty binding tools/resources/constraints to workflow steps without semantic guidance, making replay sensitive to attachment placement.
ideas.conditions: Causal explanation is the authors’ interpretation; no targeted ablation is supplied. T4, not T5, has the lowest absolute W2S score.

ideas.title: Ten observed traces are collected per enumerated W-path
ideas.statement: For every enumerated path, WSASkill collects ten traces or real interactions demonstrating the expected path behavior. These are reconstruction inputs; the reference WSA extraction is used for replay-based evaluation. A scenario type means a distinct WSA path or use case, not a raw dialogue turn.
ideas.conditions: The paper describes path-based sampling for workflow-bearing skills; construction for non-workflow cases and trace-source composition are not detailed.

ideas.title: Trace2Skill consolidates trajectory-local lessons
ideas.statement: Trace2Skill analyzes multiple executions in parallel and consolidates trajectory-local lessons into transferable skill directories, extending human-written skills or creating new ones.

ideas.title: Trace-grounded skill induction reconstructs future procedures
ideas.statement: Trace-grounded skill induction converts historical interactions or executions, including requests, observations, reasoning, tool calls, actions, outcomes, corrections, and success/failure patterns, into reusable skill artifacts.

ideas.title: Trace-to-skill induction must retain executable requirements
ideas.statement: Historical execution traces are fragmented across scenarios, contain redundant or accidental steps, and may omit rare safety-critical operations; constructing executable skills therefore requires more than ordinary summarization.

ideas.title: Different trace signals identify different runtime requirements
ideas.statement: Requests reveal activation/scope, actions reveal order, justifications reveal decision criteria, failed/rejected paths reveal local constraints, and final responses reveal output contracts. Separating these prevents treating formatting conventions as steps or isolated decisions as global rules.

ideas.title: WSA parsing precedes skill generation
