ideas.statement: Spatial memory uses a G by G scene grid. Authors hypothesize this low-bandwidth summary retains coarse location more readily than the shape/color/category of high-entropy identity anchors required after return.
ideas.conditions: Grid size G and retained object information are not quantified.

ideas.title: Withheld-readout train/inference interpretation is ambiguous
ideas.statement: Appendix C.2 explains inject-none by removing spatial tokens at inference after training-time conditioning, while B.4 declares context handling must match training and inference. The exact scope/timing of token withholding is not resolved in the PDF.
validity_flags: Apparent tension with B.4 train/inference consistency invariant

ideas.title: Weight-only temporal importance compression
ideas.statement: Weight-only compression keeps all historical temporal positions (equivalent r=1 in length terms) while changing relative influence; assumes importance can vary with age or relevance without removing availability.

ideas.title: Temporal length pooling
ideas.statement: Length compression pools neighboring observations into fewer temporal slots, assuming adjacent observations can be combined without erasing useful memory; r=4 removes three of four temporal positions.
ideas.conditions: Pooling operator formula and boundary handling are not specified in the PDF.

ideas.title: Pool first then learn importance weights
ideas.statement: Hybrid compression first collapses neighboring raw-context frames into pooled slots without an importance signal, then learns weights on that coarsened sequence. High-value views cease to be individually addressable after pooling.
validity_flags: Averaging-out explanation not backed by direct retained-information measurement

ideas.title: Hybrid qualitative comparison is not identified in Figure 8
ideas.statement: Appendix C.3 cites Figure 8 as showing hybrid rows lose identity, but Figure 8 labels a single Comp-L column and does not identify a hybrid row; the hybrid identity-loss interpretation has quantitative VLM support but no clearly labeled corresponding visual there.
validity_flags: Figure 8 hybrid cross-reference not matched by displayed labels

ideas.title: Selective object-aware compression objective
ideas.statement: Suggested improvements include object-aware pooling, revisit-success selection or preserving a small high-value frame set while compressing redundant backgrounds. Current tested compressors do not explicitly optimize these retention objectives.

ideas.title: Legacy VideoSSM and block-wise recurrent memory
ideas.statement: Two implicit-memory instantiations are a legacy VideoSSM hybrid recurrent supplement to the backbone and a paper-aligned block-wise recurrence integrated regularly into temporal computation; they differ in where and how recurrence is structured.
ideas.conditions: Paper-aligned source and full update equations are not explicitly identified in this passage.

ideas.title: Recurrent-memory advantage needs longer-horizon tests
ideas.statement: State-Space is not established universally superior: it sacrifices replay quality and requires evaluation at longer open-domain horizons plus explicit state supervision for object/view retention.

ideas.title: State read-update-write every nth DiT block
ideas.statement: Legacy hybrid adds a recurrent gate around a standard temporal-attention path; block-wise recurrence makes every nth DiT block read carried state, update it and write back, preserving a state across chunk boundaries without explicit retrieval.
ideas.conditions: Numerical n, state dimension and exact state-update equations are unspecified.
validity_flags: Claim that individual legacy blocks bypass memory is an author interpretation

ideas.title: Proposed structural minimum for recurrent memory
ideas.statement: Authors infer that state must span a nontrivial fraction of network depth to behave as memory rather than smoothing in this regime; this is an empirical interpretation of two instantiations, not a proven necessary-depth bound.
ideas.conditions: Only two recurrence structures tested; no formal theorem or depth sweep.
validity_flags: Necessity claim exceeds directly measured two-variant comparison

ideas.title: Raw-context diminishing returns suggest compression opportunity
ideas.statement: Authors describe raw history cost as linear in K and benefit as sublinear, suggesting a nearby but unreached asymptote around K=20 and an opportunity for selective compact memory. The evidence is limited to K=1,5,20.
validity_flags: Asymptote and cost law not established by comprehensive scaling study

ideas.title: Log-based GPU-hour per step efficiency diagnostic
ideas.statement: For each representative model, average step time from latest logs is converted to GPU-hour per optimization step and paired with final Replay PSNR; both axes are normalized and equal normalized cost/quality defines the diagonal. This measures replay per step cost, not semantic return or total convergence efficiency.
ideas.conditions: Underlying CSV named in PDF; absolute cost values and normalization formula absent from printed results.

ideas.title: Compression cost-control prose lacks consistent plotted advantage
ideas.statement: C.4 describes compression as trading quality for cheaper steps, but Figure 9 places Comp-L at the largest normalized per-step cost of displayed rows and excludes Comp-W. No absolute printed cost table resolves the tension; do not infer tested compression is faster than raw context.
validity_flags: Compression cheaper-step implication not established by displayed plot

ideas.title: Application-specific memory choices
ideas.statement: Authors propose compact spatial summaries for lowest-cost high-fidelity recorded-trajectory replay, block-wise recurrence for interactive repeated scene returns, and raw K=20 as a robust default when cost is secondary. These are recommendations from a small controlled matrix, not universal optima.
ideas.conditions: Application suggestions; in-domain dominance claim separately flagged and unvalidated.

ideas.title: Compression replay comparison in conclusion is metric-dependent
ideas.statement: C.7 says length r=4 is worse than hybrid r=4 on Replay, but Tables 5/10 show length r=4 better PSNR (9.88 vs 9.63) and LPIPS (.714 vs .730), while hybrid is better SSIM (.215 vs .183). Broad worse-on-Replay wording is not supported across the bundle.
validity_flags: Concluding prose inconsistent with most tabulated replay metrics

ideas.title: Do not interpret small open-domain differences strongly
ideas.statement: With eight cases per row, authors advise not over-interpreting open-domain VLM differences within roughly five points. Mechanism rankings may change with larger compute or data; the paper treats separation of evaluation axes as more durable.
ideas.conditions: Rough author caution, not a calculated confidence interval or significance threshold.

ideas.title: Verbose agent histories exceed effective context capacity
ideas.statement: Long-horizon histories combine long tool outputs, failed attempts, redundant observations and reasoning; the authors argue that these can exceed effective context capacity even with nominal million-token windows.

ideas.title: ACM separates working context from persistent raw history
ideas.statement: ACM lets the agent decide when and how to summarize and offload context, while querying an external memory on demand; in-context messages act as working memory and the external store as long-term memory.
ideas.conditions: Within an individual agentic task; inspired by Atkinson–Shiffrin memory and MemGPT.

ideas.title: Adversarial accuracy-drop metric
ideas.statement: Delta_robust = (1/N) sum_i [I(f(x_i)=y_i) - I(f(x_i_adv)=y_i)], equivalently clean accuracy minus adversarial accuracy.
ideas.conditions: Lower drop is treated as greater robustness. A smaller drop may also accompany collapsed clean accuracy; clean and adversarial accuracy must be examined together.

ideas.title: Adult income fairness evaluation
ideas.statement: Adult income records contain 14 attributes and a binary income-above-$50K label. Fairness is evaluated across race, sex and age using demographic parity difference and equalized odds difference.
ideas.conditions: Demographic parity compares positive-prediction proportions regardless of true label; equalized odds reports the larger group gap in true-positive or false-positive rates. Lower values indicate smaller measured disparities.

ideas.title: Clean versus adversarial classification evaluation
ideas.statement: SST-2 sentiment, QQP paraphrase and MNLI inference are evaluated on GLUE and AdvGLUE++; cited attacks include TextBugger, TextFooler and SememePSO, which aim to preserve semantics while inducing errors.
ideas.conditions: The source attributes TextFooler to Kwon (2023); that unusual bibliographic attribution is preserved rather than silently corrected.

ideas.title: Task adaptation does not worsen every adversarial task
ideas.statement: Math tuning Base 7B raises SST-2 drop 0.14 to 34.54 and MNLI 4.70 to 9.50 but lowers QQP 9.90 to 0.97. Math tuning Base 13B raises SST-2 18.78 to 25.79 and MNLI 6.80 to 24.59 but lowers QQP 37.51 to 6.76.
ideas.conditions: Table 7 values are percentage-point accuracy drops. Chat 13B has lower QQP drop (32.63) than Base 13B (37.51), another exception to blanket Chat-vulnerability claims. Separate clean/adversarial accuracies are absent.

ideas.title: Attribution profile for LLaMA-2 Base 13B
ideas.statement: The four largest mean layer-type sensitivities are embed_tokens 0.0231, down_proj 0.0137, k_proj 0.0107, q_proj 0.0070. In MNLI down_proj 0.0092 exceeds embed_tokens 0.0070, so highest-average embedding is not highest for every task.
ideas.conditions: Table 15; arithmetic mean of SST-2, QQP and MNLI attribution sensitivities, not prediction accuracy or intervention effect.

ideas.title: Attribution profile for LLaMA-2 Base 7B
ideas.statement: The four largest mean layer-type sensitivities are embed_tokens 0.1893, gate_proj 0.0372, down_proj 0.0294, up_proj 0.0282. In QQP down_proj 0.0354 exceeds embed_tokens 0.0200, while MNLI embedding sensitivity 0.5232 dominates.
ideas.conditions: Table 14; arithmetic mean of SST-2, QQP and MNLI attribution sensitivities, not prediction accuracy or intervention effect.

ideas.title: Attribution profile for LLaMA-2 Chat 13B
ideas.statement: The four largest mean layer-type sensitivities are embed_tokens 0.0138, down_proj 0.0085, k_proj 0.0063, q_proj 0.0050. Embedding is highest in all three tasks; down_proj is next for SST-2, QQP and MNLI.
ideas.conditions: Table 13; arithmetic mean of SST-2, QQP and MNLI attribution sensitivities, not prediction accuracy or intervention effect.

ideas.title: Attribution profile for LLaMA-2 Chat 7B
ideas.statement: The four largest mean layer-type sensitivities are embed_tokens 0.2733, gate_proj 0.0609, up_proj 0.0335, down_proj 0.0276. Embedding is highest in all three tasks; MNLI embedding sensitivity is 0.7210 versus SST-2 0.0588 and QQP 0.0402.
ideas.conditions: Table 12; arithmetic mean of SST-2, QQP and MNLI attribution sensitivities, not prediction accuracy or intervention effect.

ideas.title: Attribution profile for LLaMA-2 math-tuned Base 13B
ideas.statement: The four largest mean layer-type sensitivities are embed_tokens 0.0183, down_proj 0.0170, k_proj 0.0086, q_proj 0.0056. For SST-2 down_proj 0.0257 exceeds embedding 0.0173.
ideas.conditions: Table 17; mean over SST-2, QQP and MNLI, with full matrix retained as evidence. Fine-tuned Base models only.

ideas.title: Attribution profile for LLaMA-2 math-tuned Base 7B
ideas.statement: The four largest mean layer-type sensitivities are embed_tokens 0.0444, gate_proj 0.0123, down_proj 0.0104, up_proj 0.0085. For SST-2 k_proj 0.0131 exceeds embedding 0.0087; MNLI embedding 0.1118 remains highest.
ideas.conditions: Table 16; mean over SST-2, QQP and MNLI, with full matrix retained as evidence. Fine-tuned Base models only.

ideas.title: Attribution profile for LLaMA-2 programming-tuned Base 13B
ideas.statement: The four largest mean layer-type sensitivities are embed_tokens 0.0200, down_proj 0.0197, k_proj 0.0068, q_proj 0.0053. For SST-2 down_proj 0.0297 exceeds embedding 0.0208; mean down_proj and embedding are close.
ideas.conditions: Table 19; mean over SST-2, QQP and MNLI, with full matrix retained as evidence. Fine-tuned Base models only.

ideas.title: Attribution profile for LLaMA-2 programming-tuned Base 7B
ideas.statement: The four largest mean layer-type sensitivities are embed_tokens 0.1592, gate_proj 0.0453, up_proj 0.0322, down_proj 0.0266. Embedding is highest on all three tasks, with MNLI embedding sensitivity 0.3730.
ideas.conditions: Table 18; mean over SST-2, QQP and MNLI, with full matrix retained as evidence. Fine-tuned Base models only.

ideas.title: Clean-adversarial attribution sensitivity
ideas.statement: Layer sensitivity Delta_i = |a_i_clean - a_i_adv| measures how much an input perturbation changes that layer’s attribution score.
ideas.conditions: Requires paired GLUE and AdvGLUE++ examples; computed for SST-2, QQP and MNLI. High sensitivity is observational layer influence, not demonstrated causal protection under compression.

ideas.title: BASEL compression baseline
ideas.statement: BASEL is used as a semantically guided low-rank compression baseline in the trustworthiness experiments.
ideas.conditions: The three selected methods span the paper’s algebraic, importance-weighted and semantically guided categories.

ideas.title: Compression comparison baselines appear mislabeled
ideas.statement: Table 5 entries labeled Base 13B and Base 7B reproduce the Math Base leakage values from Tables 3–4. Figure 5 adversarial differences likewise reconcile with Math Base 13B drops (25.79/6.76/24.59), rather than Base 13B (18.78/37.51/6.80) from Table 7.
ideas.conditions: This prevents unambiguous attribution of compression deltas to an unadapted versus math-adapted source model. Preserve all original labels and numeric entries; the intended provenance requires author clarification.

ideas.title: PII privacy depends strongly on demonstrated behavior
ideas.statement: Chat models generally show low PII leakage with protected demonstrations but substantial leakage with attack demonstrations; task fine-tuning has mixed effects. Base 13B attack leakage is 33.5% versus 0.1/0.6% after math/programming adaptation; Chat 13B attack leakage is 34.8% versus 31.7/22.2% after adaptation.
ideas.conditions: Figure 3(b); Chat 7B is an exception to uniformly high attack leakage (1.8% original, rising to 29.6/25.9% after math/programming). Instruction-following is the authors’ proposed explanation.

ideas.title: Chat models disclose fewer training email addresses
ideas.statement: LLaMA-2 Chat has far lower measured training email leakage than Base at L=50/100/200; Base leakage increases with context length while Chat remains near zero.
ideas.conditions: Authors propose alignment training as an explanation; the experiment does not isolate alignment causally.

ideas.title: Retained-rank effects on accuracy drop are nonmonotonic
ideas.conditions: Table 8, LLaMA-2 compression. Negative drops mean adversarial accuracy exceeds clean accuracy, not perfect robust accuracy. No separate accuracy denominators, uncertainty intervals or floor checks are supplied.

ideas.title: Fairness degradation varies strongly by low-rank method
ideas.statement: At k=50, BASEL stays near the full model on MDPD/MEOD (+0.01/+0.02 displayed change); SVD worsens by +2.16/+2.73 and FWSVD by +0.01/+16.62.
ideas.conditions: Figure 5 LLaMA-2 Base 13B reference; positive differences denote increased measured unfairness.

ideas.title: Low email recovery after compression is not explained by high refusal
ideas.statement: All compressed Table 5 models have email leakage below 0.8%, yet rejection rates range only 0.0601%–1.3363%; low recovery therefore need not mean privacy-preserving refusal.
ideas.conditions: Enron L=200; BASEL-70 has 0.0017% leakage and 0.0601% rejection, contrasting with high rejection of uncompressed Chat models. The mechanism remains unproven.

ideas.title: Low-rank PII effects reverse with prompting setting
ideas.statement: At k=50, compression increases PII leakage in zero-shot and few-shot protected prompting but slightly reduces leakage with attack demonstrations. Displayed zero-shot/protected/attack changes are BASEL +36.75/+24.00/-0.92, SVD +50.91/+25.88/-4.06, FWSVD +43.50/+21.80/-4.06.
ideas.conditions: LLaMA-2 Base 13B reference in Figure 5 and Table 6; differences are percentage points. Safety and instruction-following disruption are proposed mechanisms rather than isolated causes.

ideas.title: Robustness changes depend on compression method and task
ideas.statement: Figure 5 reports accuracy-drop changes for SST-2/QQP/MNLI of BASEL -12.33/+4.45/-18.22, SVD -6.17/+3.18/-27.83 and FWSVD +4.38/+6.83/-1.69; BASEL and SVD improve the drop metric on two of three tasks, while all three worsen QQP.
ideas.conditions: k=50; Figure 5 names Base 13B but its differences numerically use Math Base 13B from Table 7. Relative to unadapted Base 13B, all three k=50 models have smaller QQP drops; baseline labeling materially changes interpretation.

ideas.title: Few-shot examples partly recover compressed ethical classification
ideas.statement: At k=50, displayed zero-shot/few-shot accuracy changes are BASEL -39.45/-3.70, SVD -40.08/-6.40 and FWSVD -39.22/-12.09 relative to LLaMA-2 Base 13B. All lose ethical accuracy, but few-shot demonstrations mitigate much of the zero-shot loss.
ideas.conditions: ETHICS short commonsense cases with definitive responses; the authors interpret this as weakened alignment, not directly measured alignment circuitry.

ideas.title: Compression reduces reported training email leakage
ideas.statement: All three 50%-retention LLaMA-2 Base 13B compressions report lower training-data leakage than the full reference; Figure 5 displays changes of -3.96 for BASEL, -3.97 for SVD and -3.64 for FWSVD.
ideas.conditions: Figure 5 changes equal percentage-point differences against the Table 5 3.9901% baseline, but that baseline labeled Base 13B matches Math Base 13B elsewhere. Compression-source provenance is ambiguous.

ideas.title: Email leakage reduction is not uniformly monotonic in retained rank
ideas.statement: At L=200, BASEL leakage is 0.0017% at k=70 and 0.0300% at k=50; FWSVD falls from 0.7883% to 0.3503%; SVD falls from 0.1051% to 0.0200%. Thus the claim that lower k always improves email privacy has a BASEL exception.
ideas.conditions: Table 5 labels its 13B/7B baseline leakage 3.9901/1.5031%, which matches Math Base in Tables 3–4 rather than unadapted Base. BASEL/SVD k=70 both show zero exact address recovery, with residual domain leakage.

ideas.title: Compression severity trends are metric-dependent
ideas.statement: Appendix D.5 says reduced k generally improves email leakage and adversarial drop, degrades ethics and fairness, and raises PII leakage in zero-shot/protected settings with mixed attack-setting effects.
ideas.conditions: Authors’ qualitative summary; detailed Tables 5/8/9/11 reveal nonmonotonic exceptions including BASEL email leakage and FWSVD equalized odds. Trend is not a universal monotonic law.

ideas.title: Condition number as a robustness-related quantity
ideas.statement: The source defines kappa(W)=s_max/s_min and attributes to Savostianova et al. a robustness characterization using products of condition numbers of weights and activations.
ideas.conditions: s_max and s_min are largest and smallest singular values; finite standard condition number needs a nonzero smallest singular value.

ideas.title: Benchmark mapping to trust dimensions
ideas.statement: The evaluation maps Enron Email to privacy, GLUE/AdvGLUE++ to clean/adversarial classification, ETHICS to ethics, and UCI Adult to fairness.
ideas.conditions: Four benchmark groups; Enron contains over 600,000 emails from approximately 150 users and serves as an email-data privacy proxy.

ideas.title: Low-rank efficiency measurements reused from BASEL work
ideas.statement: For LLaMA-2 7B on GSM8K with one NVIDIA A100, the source reports 23.95 GiB and 261.7 tokens/s uncompressed; SVD at 8% of original parameter count exceeds 600 tokens/s with 4.39 GiB, and prose gives BASEL throughput 621.9 tokens/s.
ideas.conditions: Figure 6 caption explicitly credits Li et al. (2025a) as the source of the results; this is background reused evidence, not newly established measurements. Prose says BASEL is fastest, but the plotted leftmost FWSVD point appears higher.

ideas.title: Task adaptation reduces Chat email refusals
ideas.statement: At L=200, Chat 7B rejects 77.11% of email requests versus 33.62% after math and 59.39% after programming; Chat 13B rejects 58.09% versus 36.04% and 46.13%. Base variants reject at most 0.33% at L=200.
ideas.conditions: Tables 3–4; non-rejection does not imply correct recovery. Fine-tuned Chat leakage remains much lower than most Base variants despite reduced refusal.

ideas.title: Short commonsense morality classification
ideas.statement: The standard ethics test uses short test samples from ETHICS commonsense morality and asks for wrong/not wrong under zero-shot and few-shot demonstrations. Accuracy is computed only for definitive responses.
ideas.conditions: The commonsense subset has 13,910 training and 3,885 total test samples, including long narratives; evaluation restricts to short cases. The five ETHICS dimensions are commonsense morality, deontology, justice, utilitarianism and virtue ethics.

ideas.title: Compression severity does not monotonically affect both fairness gaps
ideas.conditions: All listed compressed models have larger gaps than full Base 13B. However, SVD MEOD improves from k=70 to 50 and FWSVD MEOD improves from 50 to 30, qualifying monotonic-degradation prose. Aggregation across three sensitive attributes is not specified in the result table.

ideas.title: Few-shot ethics gains and losses depend on retained rank
ideas.statement: Zero-shot ethics falls monotonically with lower k for SVD (41.87/12.84/5.01%), FWSVD (37.80/13.70/6.27%) and BASEL (38.45/13.47/7.48%) at k=70/50/30. Few-shot scores are SVD 64.77/56.71/53.44%, FWSVD 77.15/51.02/41.87%, BASEL 60.36/59.41/17.92%.
ideas.conditions: Table 9; full Base 13B zero/few-shot is 52.92/63.11%. Mild SVD/FWSVD compression with few-shot examples exceeds the full few-shot baseline, so the broad claim all compressed ethics is worse is restricted to k=50 or stronger examples. Accuracy conditions on definitive answers.

ideas.title: Task fine-tuning does not consistently remove email leakage
ideas.statement: At L=200, Base 7B leakage is 2.119%, math 1.503%, programming 3.013%; Base 13B is 1.905%, math 3.990%, programming 1.932%. Chat 7B values are 0.005/0.384/0.023% and Chat 13B 0.020/0.707/0.077% for original/math/programming.
ideas.conditions: Figure 3(a) aggregate email leakage; variable changes show no consistent privacy improvement under task adaptation.

ideas.title: Scale and task fine-tuning often increase adversarial accuracy drop
ideas.statement: LLaMA-2 Chat and task-fine-tuned variants generally have larger clean-to-adversarial accuracy drops than Base; larger 13B models are not consistently more robust than 7B.
ideas.conditions: SST-2, QQP and MNLI; qualitative aggregate trend with task/model exceptions. Table 7 supplies accuracy-drop values but not separate clean and adversarial accuracies.

ideas.title: Task adaptation sharply raises jailbreak false positive rates
ideas.statement: LLaMA-2 Base 7B mean jailbreak FPR increases from 10.20% to 91.80% after math fine-tuning; several Chat task-adapted variants exceed 90%. Chat variants generally show more jailbreak false acceptance than Base.
ideas.conditions: Five fixed jailbreak instructions on immoral ETHICS scenarios; averaged FPR. Attribution to instruction tuning is interpretive rather than a controlled causal finding.

ideas.title: FWSVD compression baseline
ideas.statement: FWSVD is used as a importance-weighted low-rank compression baseline in the trustworthiness experiments.
ideas.conditions: The three selected methods span the paper’s algebraic, importance-weighted and semantically guided categories.

ideas.title: Black-box inference threat model
ideas.statement: A compressed or task-fine-tuned model is deployed on a user device. An attacker can query its input-output interface and may know architecture, training procedure or public pretraining data, but cannot alter internal model weights.
ideas.conditions: Assets include conversation confidentiality, robust predictions, ethical alignment and group fairness. Prompt filters and safety alignment are not assumed to remain comprehensive after compression.

ideas.title: Jailbreak-induced false moral acceptance
ideas.statement: Five instructions from Wang et al. (2023a) are embedded into standard ethics prompts; FPR is the fraction of immoral scenarios wrongly judged not wrong. Higher FPR means weaker resistance to these jailbreaks.
ideas.conditions: An ethical classification benchmark with five fixed instructions, not a general harmful-generation safety evaluation.

ideas.title: Five fixed ethical override templates
ideas.statement: The benchmark uses five templates: adopting an immoral assistant persona, classifying every reaction as not wrong, disclaiming alignment with human morality, preferring wrong reactions as not wrong, and requesting a jailbreaking answer.
ideas.conditions: Appendix D.3 lists templates as research attack data; this extraction records their role and does not execute them. FPR averages all five.

ideas.title: Gradient-times-activation layer attribution
ideas.statement: Using a first-order Taylor approximation to loss when suppressing hidden activation h_i, the paper defines a_i = ||(partial ell/partial h_i) h_i||_2 as layer attribution.
ideas.conditions: h_i=Layer_i(h_(i-1)); h_0=x. This is a local first-order sensitivity heuristic; the paper writes the product without explicitly specifying componentwise contraction details.

ideas.title: Reduced representational capacity may suppress exact data recovery
ideas.statement: The authors explain reduced email recovery by citing capacity-dependent memorization and arguing that low-rank restriction preserves less detailed sequence information.
ideas.conditions: Qualitative mechanism consistent with observations; cites Carlini 2021/2023 and does not derive or test a quantitative compression-to-memorization law.

ideas.title: Complementary model compression families
ideas.statement: Quantization reduces weight precision, pruning removes weights, and low-rank factorization decomposes large weight matrices into lower-dimensional matrices to reduce model resource demands.
ideas.conditions: Background distinctions for model-weight compression, rather than a prompt-compression algorithm.

ideas.title: Model and task-adaptation design
ideas.statement: Experiments cover LLaMA-2 7B/13B Base and Chat and Qwen-2.5 7B/14B. LLaMA Base/Chat 7B/13B and Qwen 7B are fine-tuned for mathematics and code generation. Compression is applied to LLaMA-2 13B Base and Qwen-2.5 7B.
ideas.conditions: Comparative empirical design across two model families; the paper does not establish universal generalization.

ideas.title: Partial address recovery exceeds exact email recovery
ideas.statement: For original Base models at L=200, exact/local/domain recovery is 0.72/2.93/2.71% (7B) and 0.60/2.00/3.11% (13B); near-zero exact Chat recovery can coexist with small domain recovery.
ideas.conditions: Tables 3–4; aggregate leakage is the mean of full/local/domain recovery, not the percentage of prompts leaking any component.

ideas.title: Stronger compression worsens zero-shot and protected PII leakage
ideas.statement: From k=70 to 50, zero-shot/protected leakage rises from 42.00/21.42 to 42.42/27.33% for BASEL, 26.25/13.25 to 49.17/25.13% for FWSVD, and 47.25/23.63 to 56.58/29.21% for SVD. Attack leakage rises slightly for BASEL (30.94 to 32.61%) but falls for FWSVD (34.31 to 29.47%) and SVD (31.52 to 29.47%).
ideas.conditions: Table 6; full Base 13B zero-shot/protected/attack leakage 5.67/3.33/33.53%. Protected refusal also falls for all three methods when k drops, and zero-shot rejection is at most 0.25%.

ideas.title: Conversation PII disclosure under three prompt settings
ideas.statement: The test puts names and identifiers into prompts and then queries their disclosure. Zero-shot requests PII without examples; few-shot protected examples demonstrate refusal; few-shot attack examples demonstrate successful disclosure. Leakage and rejection rates are reported.
ideas.conditions: Names, social security numbers, email addresses and phone numbers are included. This tests conversation confidentiality, distinct from training-data recovery.

ideas.title: Contextual prompting as a possible trustworthiness intervention
ideas.statement: Because trustworthiness depends strongly on contextual prompting, the authors suggest prompt engineering as a potential route to improve trust in compressed models and invite deeper studies beyond this broad evaluation.
ideas.conditions: Proposal, not a demonstrated prompt-compression method or validated intervention.

ideas.title: Qwen replication covers only selected trust dimensions
ideas.statement: The Qwen-2.5 extension evaluates training-data privacy and adversarial accuracy drop, with SVD compression of 7B and comparisons to 14B/task-adapted 7B.
ideas.conditions: It does not replicate conversational PII confidentiality, ethics or fairness across Qwen, and does not compare FWSVD/BASEL there. Broad cross-family claims are limited to the evaluated aspects.

ideas.title: Qwen scale and task adaptation generally increase adversarial drop
ideas.statement: Qwen 7B SST-2/QQP/MNLI drops are 21.9/63.4/23.7%, versus 14B 26.2/63.9/33.9; math 7B 22.7/61.5/35.1 and programming 7B 24.0/64.4/30.3.
ideas.conditions: Table 22; mathematical adaptation improves the QQP drop slightly, but worsens SST-2/MNLI. Separate absolute accuracies and uncertainty estimates are not reported.

ideas.title: Qwen SVD compression sharply lowers measured adversarial drop
ideas.statement: Qwen-2.5 7B SVD at k=70 has SST-2/QQP/MNLI drops 2.31/1.17/16.17%, and k=50 has 0.015/0.020/2.33%, versus full 7B 21.9/63.4/23.7%.
ideas.conditions: Table 22; supports smaller clean-adversarial differences across all three tasks, but does not establish higher absolute attacked accuracy because the table omits clean/attacked accuracies.

ideas.title: SVD reduces Qwen email recovery without raising refusal
ideas.statement: Qwen-2.5 7B aggregate email leakage at L=200 is 0.4404%, falling to 0.0033% at SVD k=70 and 0.0000% at k=50. Rejection falls from 5.2903% to 0.1401% and 0.0890%.
ideas.conditions: Table 21: original exact/local/domain recovery is 0.0651/0.5405/0.7157%; at k=70 only domain recovery 0.0100% remains; at k=50 all three are zero. Zero measured leakage is restricted to this test and is not a privacy guarantee.

ideas.title: Truncated-basis refusal reconstruction error
ideas.statement: Under an orthonormal singular basis, the closest representable refusal vector in the top-r-prime span is v_hat=sum_(k<=r-prime) lambda_k u_k, and squared error ||v-v_hat||²=sum_(k>r-prime) lambda_k².
ideas.conditions: The minimizer matches all retained coefficients. The proof separates retained coefficient-error squares from the fixed discarded-coefficient sum; this is a conditional linear projection identity.

ideas.title: Lower retained rank cannot reduce refusal projection error
ideas.statement: For i<=j, the squared refusal-vector projection error retaining i directions is at least that retaining j directions, because discarded coefficient squares form nested nonnegative tail sums. The authors infer that stronger truncation may weaken successful refusal.
ideas.conditions: Error is non-decreasing, not necessarily strictly increasing: discarded coefficients can be zero. The algebra does not itself establish a probability-of-refusal law or network-wide safety degradation.

ideas.title: Refusal represented in a retained weight-output subspace
ideas.statement: Building on Arditi et al., the paper assumes a safety subspace S within span(u_1,...,u_r) of the left singular vectors of one rank-r weight matrix and expresses a refusal vector v=sum_k lambda_k u_k, lambda_k=<v,u_k>.
ideas.conditions: The assumption links a model-level refusal vector to a chosen linear weight column space. Truncating to r-prime retains only span(u_1,...,u_r-prime); nonlinear/residual compensation is outside this model.

ideas.title: Prior trustworthiness benchmarks and compression studies
ideas.statement: The paper situates itself after PII attacks on GPT-2, PromptBench adversarial evaluation, multi-perspective GPT-3.5/GPT-4 evaluation, and Hong et al.’s quantized/pruned model study.
ideas.conditions: Related-work attribution is source-reported. Its fairness claim attributed to Socher et al. (2013) is bibliographically suspect because the listed title concerns sentiment models.

ideas.title: Model scale changes prominent robustness-sensitive projections
ideas.statement: In reported 7B Base/Chat and adapted variants, feed-forward gate_proj/down_proj/up_proj dominate; 13B models additionally show prominent attention q_proj/k_proj contributions.
ideas.conditions: Section 6.2 and Appendix E Table 20; scale is correlated with this pattern, not independently manipulated architecture. Table 20 includes task-adapted Base models, not task-adapted Chat models.

ideas.title: Embedding and down projection have high attribution sensitivity
ideas.statement: The paper reports embed_tokens highest across models and down_proj within the top four; down_proj is the MLP’s final projection transmitting its nonlinear representation.
ideas.conditions: Table 20 ranks average sensitivities for eight model configurations; the highest-average embedding claim should not be read as highest on every task.

ideas.title: Compression percentage denotes retained singular-value mass
ideas.statement: The compression ratio k% is the sum of retained singular values divided by the sum of all singular values; smaller k is more aggressive compression.
ideas.conditions: The study varies k, including 70%, 50% and 30%. This is not specified as percentage of parameters or percentage of singular components retained.

ideas.title: Natural smaller model differs from compressed larger model
ideas.statement: The uncompressed Base 7B comparator shows displayed changes versus Base 13B of training leakage -2.49, PII zero/protected/attack -5.67/-2.72/-32.61, SST-2/QQP/MNLI drop +8.75/-5.79/-15.10, ethics zero/few -1.76/-8.49, and fairness MDPD/MEOD +0.16/+0.28.
ideas.conditions: Figure 5 comparative row; training-leakage and adversarial-drop baseline labels match math-adapted values elsewhere, whereas PII/ethics/fairness match listed Base models. k=50 does not necessarily mean half the parameters.

ideas.title: Four-perspective study of low-rank trustworthiness
ideas.statement: The study evaluates privacy, adversarial robustness, machine ethics and fairness under low-rank model compression, model scale and fine-tuning, and uses gradient attribution to inspect robustness-related layers.
ideas.conditions: LLaMA-2 and Qwen-2.5 models; the claim of being the first comprehensive study is the authors’ priority claim, not independently established.

ideas.title: SVD compression baseline
ideas.statement: SVD is used as a algebraic low-rank compression baseline in the trustworthiness experiments.
ideas.conditions: The three selected methods span the paper’s algebraic, importance-weighted and semantically guided categories.

ideas.title: SVD parameter reduction
ideas.statement: Approximate W in R^(n×m) by U Sigma V^T using r retained singular components, replacing nm parameters by r(n+m) parameters via U and Sigma V^T.
ideas.conditions: U is n×r, V is m×r and Sigma is diagonal r×r; substantial savings require r much smaller than min(n,m).

ideas.title: Attribution varies by task and component type
ideas.statement: The authors report embeddings as consistently most sensitive, attention slightly above MLP for SST-2, MLP above attention for MNLI, and balanced MLP/attention contributions for QQP.
ideas.conditions: Tables 12–19 report eight configurations. Embedding is top by cross-task average, but QQP Base 7B, MNLI Base 13B and several tuned SST-2 cases have a projection above embedding. Broad attention/MLP task trends are also not universal.

ideas.title: Contextual email-recovery privacy test
ideas.statement: Training-data leakage is evaluated by prompting with 50, 100 or 200 tokens preceding a target email address and measuring exact address, local username and domain recovery. Aggregate leakage rate is the arithmetic mean of these three percentages; rejection is refusal to provide any email address.
ideas.conditions: L is preceding context length; Enron is used as a realistic proxy. Recovery is an operational measure and does not itself prove how data entered the model.

ideas.title: Discarding small singular directions is proposed to improve robustness
ideas.statement: The authors argue that discarding small singular values raises the retained minimum and lowers a condition-number-based sensitivity measure, explaining smaller adversarial accuracy drops.
ideas.conditions: This reasoning applies to the retained nonzero singular subspace. A rank-deficient full matrix has zero singular values and standard condition number is infinite/undefined, so the paper’s unqualified full-matrix claim requires qualification; empirical accuracy-drop reduction is not a guarantee.

ideas.title: Operational examples of trustworthiness failures
ideas.statement: The illustrative failures distinguish training email recovery, disclosure of conversation-provided PII, a semantically equivalent question misclassified after a typo, an immoral scenario labeled not wrong, and changed income predictions across sex.
ideas.conditions: Figure 1 examples illustrate the evaluation perspectives; they are not prevalence estimates or commands for the reader.

ideas.title: Benign accuracy alone misses trustworthiness trade-offs
ideas.statement: The authors summarize low-rank compression as improving training-data privacy and adversarial robustness but worsening PII confidentiality, ethics and fairness; deployment assessment therefore needs multiple trust metrics alongside benign accuracy.
ideas.conditions: Directional synthesis of selected experiments, with task/method/prompt exceptions retained in atomic result records.
